entries.literal: Plucked zheng, strummed zheng, horizontal and vertical konghou, pipa, five-string, sheng, xiao, bili, small bili, di, transverse di, waist drum, Qi drum, eaves drum—each one.

entries.zh: 銅鈸二，貝一。
entries.en: Two bronze cymbals, one shell horn.
entries.literal: Two bronze cymbals, one shell.

entries.zh: 白舞一人，方舞四人。
entries.en: One white dance, four square dance.
entries.literal: One white dance, four square dance.

entries.zh: 天竺伎，有銅鼓、羯鼓、都曇鼓、毛員鼓、觱篥、橫笛、鳳首箜篌、琵琶、五絃、貝，皆一；
entries.en: Indic: one each bronze, jie, Dutun, Maoyuan drums, bili, transverse di, phoenix konghou, pipa, five-string, shell.
entries.literal: Indic performers: bronze drum, jie drum, Dutun drum, Maoyuan drum, bili, transverse di, phoenix-head konghou, pipa, five-string, shell—each one.

entries.zh: 銅鈸二，舞者二人。
entries.en: Two cymbals, two dancers.
entries.literal: Two bronze cymbals, two dancers.

entries.zh: 高麗伎，有彈箏、搊箏、鳳首箜篌、臥箜篌、豎箜篌、琵琶，以蛇皮為槽，厚寸餘，有鱗甲，楸木為面，象牙為捍撥，畫國王形。
entries.en: Koryo: plucked and strummed zheng, phoenix and horizontal konghou, pipa with snake-skin box an inch thick scaled, catalpa face, ivory guard painted with the king.
entries.literal: Koryo performers: plucked zheng, strummed zheng, phoenix konghou, horizontal and vertical konghou, pipa with snake-skin soundbox an inch thick with scale pattern, catalpa face, ivory plectrum guard painted with the king's image.

entries.zh: 又有五絃、義觜笛、笙、葫蘆笙、簫、小觱篥、桃皮觱篥、腰鼓、齊鼓、檐鼓、龜頭鼓、鐵版、貝、大觱篥。
entries.en: Also five-string, yizui di, sheng, gourd sheng, xiao, bili large and small, many drums, iron clapper, shell, great bili.
entries.literal: Also five-string, yizui di, sheng, gourd sheng, xiao, small bili, peach-skin bili, waist, Qi, eaves, turtle-head, and great drums, iron clapper, shell, great bili.

entries.zh: 胡旋舞，舞者立毬上，旋轉如風。
entries.en: Hu Xuan dance: dancers spin atop a ball like wind.
entries.literal: Hu Xuan dance: dancers stand on a ball and spin like wind.

entries.zh: 龜茲伎，有彈箏、豎箜篌、琵琶、五絃、橫笛、笙、簫、觱篥、答臘鼓、毛員鼓、都曇鼓、侯提鼓、雞婁鼓、腰鼓、齊鼓、檐鼓、貝，皆一；
entries.en: Kucha: one each plucked zheng, vertical konghou, pipa, five-string, transverse di, sheng, xiao, bili, dalagu, Maoyuan, Dutun, houti, jilou, waist, Qi, eaves drums, shell.
entries.literal: Kucha performers: plucked zheng, vertical konghou, pipa, five-string, transverse di, sheng, xiao, bili, dalagu, Maoyuan, Dutun, houti, jilou, waist, Qi, eaves drums, shell—each one.

entries.zh: 銅鈸二。
entries.en: Two bronze cymbals.
entries.literal: Two bronze cymbals.

entries.zh: 舞者四人。
entries.en: Four dancers.
entries.literal: Four dancers.

entries.zh: 設五方師子，高丈餘，飾以方色。
entries.en: Five directional lions over a zhang tall, colored by direction.
entries.literal: Five direction lions over a zhang high, decorated in directional colors.

entries.zh: 每師子有十二人，畫衣，執紅拂，首加紅袜，謂之師子郎。
entries.en: Twelve painted robe bearers with red whisks and red socks per lion—"lion lads."
entries.literal: Each lion had twelve men in painted robes holding red whisks, red socks on the head, called lion lads.

entries.zh: 安國伎，有豎箜篌、琵琶、五絃、橫笛、簫、觱篥、正鼓、和鼓、銅鈸，皆一；
entries.en: Anguo: one each vertical konghou, pipa, five-string, transverse di, xiao, bili, zheng and he drums, cymbal.
entries.literal: Anguo performers: vertical konghou, pipa, five-string, transverse di, xiao, bili, zheng drum, he drum, bronze cymbal—each one.

entries.zh: 舞者二人。
entries.en: Two dancers.
entries.literal: Two dancers.

entries.zh: 疏勒伎，有豎箜篌、琵琶、五絃、簫、橫笛、觱篥、答臘鼓、羯鼓、侯提鼓、腰鼓、雞婁鼓，皆一；
entries.en: Shule: one each vertical konghou, pipa, five-string, xiao, transverse di, bili, dalagu, jie, houti, waist, jilou drums.
entries.literal: Shule performers: vertical konghou, pipa, five-string, xiao, transverse di, bili, dalagu, jie, houti, waist, jilou drums—each one.

entries.zh: 舞者二人。
entries.en: Two dancers.
entries.literal: Two dancers.

entries.zh: 康國伎，有正鼓、和鼓，皆一；
entries.en: Kangju: one each zheng and he drums.
entries.literal: Kangju performers: zheng and he drums each one.

entries.zh: 笛、銅鈸，皆二。
entries.en: Two each di and cymbals.
entries.literal: Di and bronze cymbals each two.

entries.zh: 舞者二人。
entries.en: Two dancers.
entries.literal: Two dancers.

entries.zh: 工人之服皆從其國。
entries.en: Musicians dressed in their native styles.
entries.literal: Workers' dress followed their countries.

entries.zh: 聲無形而樂有器。
entries.en: Sound is formless, yet music requires instruments.
entries.literal: Sound has no form, yet music has instruments.

entries.zh: 古之作樂者，知夫器之必有弊，而聲不可以言傳，懼夫器失而聲遂亡也，乃多為之法以著之。
entries.en: Ancient composers knew instruments wear out and sound cannot be passed on in speech; lest instruments vanish and sound with them, they devised many ways to fix it in writing.
entries.literal: The ancients who made music knew that instruments must eventually fail and that sound cannot be handed down in words; fearing that when instruments were lost sound would perish, they devised many methods to record it.

entries.zh: 故始求聲者以律，而造律者以黍。
entries.en: Those who first pursued tone turned to pitch pipes; those who forged pitch pipes took millet as their measure.
entries.literal: Therefore those who first sought sound used pitch pipes, and those who made pitch pipes used millet.

entries.zh: 自一黍之廣，積而為分、寸；
entries.en: From the width of a single millet grain, one accumulates fen and cun.
entries.literal: From the breadth of one millet grain, accumulated into fen and cun.

entries.zh: 一黍之多，積而為龠、合；
entries.en: From the capacity of one millet grain, one accumulates yue and he.
entries.literal: From the volume of one millet grain, accumulated into yue and he.

entries.zh: 一黍之重，積而為銖、兩。
entries.en: From the weight of one millet grain, one accumulates zhu and liang.
entries.literal: From the weight of one millet grain, accumulated into zhu and liang.

entries.zh: 此造律之本也。
entries.en: Such is the foundation of pitch-pipe manufacture.
entries.literal: This is the root of making pitch pipes.

entries.zh: 故為之長短之法，而著之於度；
entries.en: They codified rules of length and fixed them in the standard of length.
entries.literal: Therefore they made methods of long and short and recorded them in measures of length.

entries.zh: 為之多少之法，而著之於量；
entries.en: They codified rules of quantity and fixed them in the standard of capacity.
entries.literal: They made methods of more and less and recorded them in measures of capacity.

entries.zh: 為之輕重之法，而著之於權衡。
entries.en: They codified rules of weight and fixed them in balances and steelyards.
entries.literal: They made methods of light and heavy and recorded them in balances and steelyards.

entries.zh: 是三物者，亦必有時而弊，則又總其法而著之於數。
entries.en: These three standards too must eventually fail; they therefore summed their rules and committed them to number.
entries.literal: These three things too must in time fail; then they gathered their methods together and recorded them in numbers.

entries.zh: 使其分寸、龠合、銖兩皆起於黃鍾，然後律、度、量、衡相用為表裏，使得律者可以制度、量、衡，因度、量、衡亦可以制律。
entries.en: Fen, cun, yue, he, zhu, and liang all derived from the Yellow Bell; pitch pipes, length, capacity, and weight then served as mutual inner and outer measures—whoever held the pipes could derive the rest, and from length, capacity, and weight one could likewise derive the pipes.
entries.literal: They made fen, cun, yue, he, zhu, and liang all arise from the Yellow Bell; then pitch pipes, length, capacity, and weight were used as inner and outer counterparts, so that one who had pitch pipes could make length, capacity, and weight, and by length, capacity, and weight one could also make pitch pipes.

entries.zh: 不幸而皆亡，則推其法數而制之，用其長短、多少、輕重以相參考。
entries.en: Should all be lost, one could still reconstruct them from their numerical rules, cross-checking length, capacity, and weight.
entries.literal: If unhappily all were lost, then one deduced from their numerical methods to make them, using their long and short, more and less, light and heavy for mutual reference.

entries.zh: 四者既同，而聲必至，聲至后樂可作矣。
entries.en: Once the four agreed, tone would surely be recovered; with tone restored, music could be composed.
entries.literal: When the four were alike, sound was bound to arrive; once sound arrived, music could then be made.

entries.zh: 夫物用於有形而必弊，聲藏於無形而不竭，以有數之法求無形之聲，其法具存。
entries.en: Material things in visible form wear out; sound dwelling in the invisible does not exhaust itself—seek the formless through numbered rules, and the rules endure entire.
entries.literal: Things used in what has form must fail; sound hidden in what has no form is inexhaustible—using methods that have number to seek sound that has no form, the methods remain fully preserved.

entries.zh: 無作則已，苟有作者，雖去聖人於千萬歲後，無不得焉。
entries.en: If none undertakes the task, so be it; yet whoever does, though ten thousand years from the sages, need miss nothing.
entries.literal: If there is no making, so be it; but if there is a maker, though separated from the sages by ten thousand years, nothing is unobtainable.

entries.zh: 此古之君子知物之終始，而憂世之慮深，其多為之法而丁寧纖悉，可謂至矣。
entries.en: The ancients, knowing how things begin and end and anxious for posterity, multiplied methods with painstaking detail—nothing could exceed it.
entries.literal: Thus the gentlemen of old, knowing things' beginning and end and deeply concerned for the age, made many methods with meticulous care—one may call this utmost.

entries.zh: 自周、陳以上，雅鄭淆雜而無別，隋文帝始分雅、俗二部，至唐更曰「部當」。
entries.en: Through the Zhou and Chen era, court and popular music ran together without clear separation until Sui Wendi split them into elegant and popular bureaus; under Tang the categories were renamed "section assignments."
entries.literal: From the Zhou and Chen [dynasties] upward, elegant and Zheng music were confused and mixed without distinction; Emperor Wen of Sui first divided them into elegant and popular two sections; in Tang they were further called "section assignments."

entries.zh: 周、隋管弦雜曲數百，皆西涼樂也。
entries.en: Zhou and Sui preserved hundreds of mixed orchestral pieces, all of Western Liang origin.
entries.literal: The hundreds of mixed orchestral pieces of Zhou and Sui were all Western Liang music.

entries.zh: 鼓舞曲，皆龜茲樂也。
entries.en: Dance pieces with drum accompaniment were Kucha in origin.
entries.literal: Drum-and-dance pieces were all Kucha music.

entries.zh: 唯琴工猶傳楚、漢舊聲及《清調》，蔡邕五弄、楚調四弄，謂之九弄。
entries.en: Only qin masters still carried Chu and Han legacy tunes and the Clear Mode—Cai Yong's five suites plus the Chu mode's four, known together as the Nine Suites.
entries.literal: Only qin players still transmitted old Chu and Han sounds and the "Clear Mode"; Cai Yong's five suites and the Chu mode's four suites were called the nine suites.

entries.zh: 隋亡，清樂散缺，存者才六十三曲。
entries.en: After Sui's collapse clear music broke apart; barely sixty-three pieces remained.
entries.literal: When Sui fell, clear music scattered and was lost; only sixty-three pieces survived.

entries.zh: 其後傳者：《平調》、《清調》，周《房中樂》遺聲也；
entries.en: Pieces still handed down included Plain Mode and Clear Mode, Zhou survivals from inner-chamber music;
entries.literal: Those transmitted later: "Plain Mode" and "Clear Mode" are survivals of Zhou inner-chamber music;

entries.zh: 《白雪》，楚曲也；
entries.en: "White Snow," a Chu melody;
entries.literal: "White Snow" is a Chu tune;

entries.zh: 《公莫舞》，漢舞也；
entries.en: "Lord, do not!" a Han dance piece;
entries.literal: "Lord, do not!" is a Han dance;

entries.zh: 《巴渝》，漢高帝命工人作也；
entries.en: "Bayu," commissioned by Han Gaozu from his artisans;
entries.literal: "Bayu" was made when Emperor Gaozu of Han ordered craftsmen to compose it;

entries.zh: 《明君》，漢元帝時作也；
entries.en: "Bright Lady," from Han Yuandi's reign;
entries.literal: "Bright Lady" was composed in the time of Emperor Yuan of Han;

entries.zh: 《明之君》，漢《鞞舞》曲也；
entries.en: "Bright Lord," a Han shield-dance tune;
entries.literal: "Bright Lord" is a Han "Shield Dance" tune;

entries.zh: 《鐸舞》，漢曲也；
entries.en: "Duo Dance," Han in origin;
entries.literal: "Duo Dance" is a Han tune;

entries.zh: 《白鳩》，吳《拂舞》曲也；
entries.en: "White Dove," from Wu's whisk dance;
entries.literal: "White Dove" is a Wu "Whisk Dance" tune;

entries.zh: 《白紵》，吳舞也；
entries.en: "White Ramie," a Wu dance;
entries.literal: "White Ramie" is a Wu dance;

entries.zh: 《子夜》，晉曲也；
entries.en: "Midnight," Jin;
entries.literal: "Midnight" is a Jin tune;

entries.zh: 《前溪》，晉車騎將軍沈珫作也；
entries.en: "Front Brook," by Jin General of Chariots and Cavalry Shen Chong;
entries.literal: "Front Brook" was composed by Jin General of Chariots and Cavalry Shen Chong;

entries.zh: 《團扇》，晉王瑉歌也；
entries.en: "Round Fan," a song by Jin Wang Min;
entries.literal: "Round Fan" is a song by Jin Wang Min;

entries.zh: 《懊儂》，晉隆安初謠也；
entries.en: "Regretful Lover," a ballad from early Jin Long'an;
entries.literal: "Regretful Lover" is a ballad from early Long'an of Jin;

entries.zh: 《長史變》，晉司徒左長史王廞作也；
entries.en: "Chief Clerk Variation," by Jin Left Chief Clerk Wang Xin;
entries.literal: "Chief Clerk Variation" was composed by Jin Left Chief Clerk of the Minister Wang Xin;

entries.zh: 《丁督護》，晉、宋間曲也；
entries.en: "Ding, the Chief Steward," from the Jin–Song interval;
entries.literal: "Ding, the Chief Steward" is a tune from between Jin and Song;

entries.zh: 《讀曲》，宋人為彭城王義康作也；
entries.en: "Reading Tune," composed in Song for Prince of Pengcheng Yikang;
entries.literal: "Reading Tune" was made by a Song man for Prince of Pengcheng Yikang;

entries.zh: 《烏夜啼》，宋臨川王義慶作也；
entries.en: "Crow Cries at Night," by Song Prince of Linchuan Yiqing;
entries.literal: "Crow Cries at Night" was composed by Song Prince of Linchuan Yiqing;

entries.zh: 《石城》，宋臧質作也；
entries.en: "Stone City," by Song Zang Zhi;
entries.literal: "Stone City" was composed by Song Zang Zhi;

entries.zh: 《莫愁》《石城樂》所出也；
entries.en: "Mochou" grew out of "Stone City Music";
entries.literal: "Mochou" derives from "Stone City Music";

entries.zh: 《襄陽》，宋隨王誕作也；
entries.en: "Xiangyang," by Song Prince of Sui Dan;
entries.literal: "Xiangyang" was composed by Song Prince of Sui Wang Dan;

entries.zh: 《烏夜飛》，宋沈攸之作也；
entries.en: "Crow Flies at Night," by Song Shen Youzhi;
entries.literal: "Crow Flies at Night" was composed by Song Shen Youzhi;

entries.zh: 《估客樂》，齊武帝作也；
entries.en: "Merchant's Song," by Qi Emperor Wu;
entries.literal: "Merchant's Song" was composed by Qi Emperor Wu;

entries.zh: 《楊叛》，北齊歌也；
entries.en: "Yang the Rebel," a Northern Qi song;
entries.literal: "Yang the Rebel" is a Northern Qi song;

entries.zh: 《驍壺》，投壺樂也；
entries.en: "Valiant Pot," music for pitch-pot play;
entries.literal: "Valiant Pot" is pitch-pot music;

entries.zh: 《常林歡》，宋、梁間曲也；
entries.en: "Changlin Joy," from the Song–Liang period;
entries.literal: "Changlin Joy" is a tune from between Song and Liang;

entries.zh: 《三洲》，商人歌也；
entries.en: "Three Isles," a merchants' song;
entries.literal: "Three Isles" is a merchant's song;

entries.zh: 《採桑》，《三洲曲》所出也；
entries.en: "Picking Mulberry," spun from the Three Isles tune;
entries.literal: "Picking Mulberry" derives from the "Three Isles Tune";

entries.zh: 《玉樹後庭花》、《堂堂》，陳後主作也；
entries.en: "Jade Tree in the Rear Court" and "Stately," by Chen's last emperor;
entries.literal: "Jade Tree in the Rear Court" and "Stately" were composed by Chen Last Lord;

entries.zh: 《泛龍舟》，隋煬帝作也。
entries.en: "Floating Dragon Boat," by Sui Yangdi.
entries.literal: "Floating Dragon Boat" was composed by Emperor Yang of Sui.

entries.zh: 又有《吳聲四時歌》、《雅歌》、《上林》、《鳳雛》、《平折》、《命嘯》等曲，其聲與其辭皆訛失，十不傳其一二。
entries.en: Other titles—"Wu Sound Four Seasons Song," "Elegant Song," "Upper Grove," "Phoenix Chick," "Level Bend," "Commanding Cry"—survived only in name; music and text alike are garbled, and scarcely one piece in ten still passes down intact.
entries.literal: There were also tunes such as "Wu Sound Four Seasons Song," "Elegant Song," "Upper Grove," "Phoenix Chick," "Level Bend," and "Commanding Cry"; both their sounds and their texts are corrupted and lost—not one or two in ten are transmitted.

entries.zh: 初，隋有法曲，其音清而近雅。
entries.en: Sui had long kept the fa tune, clear-toned and close to court style.
entries.literal: At first Sui had the fa tune; its sound was clear and near to elegant.

entries.zh: 其器有鐃、鈸、鐘、磬、幢簫、琵琶。
entries.en: It used nao and bo cymbals, bells, stone chimes, banner flutes, and pipa.
entries.literal: Its instruments were nao, bo, bell, stone chime, banner flute, and pipa.

entries.zh: 琵琶圓體修頸而小，號曰「秦漢子」，蓋弦鞀之遺制，出於胡中，傳為秦、漢所作。
entries.en: The pipa is round-bodied with a long thin neck—nicknamed "Qin-Han Son," a descendant of the string drum from the frontier, credited by tradition to Qin and Han times.
entries.literal: The pipa has a round body, slender neck, and small size; it is called the "Qin-Han Son," being a legacy form of the string drum, coming from among the barbarians and handed down as the work of Qin and Han.

entries.zh: 其聲金、石、絲、竹以次作，隋煬帝厭其聲澹，曲終復加解音。
entries.en: Metal, stone, silk, and bamboo entered in turn; Sui Yangdi found the tone too plain and had ornamental figures added after every closing.
entries.literal: Its sounds of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo were performed in sequence; Emperor Yang of Sui disliked its thin sound and after each piece added embellishing tones.

entries.zh: 玄宗既知音律，又酷愛法曲，選坐部伎子弟三百教於梨園，聲有誤者，帝必覺而正之，號「皇帝梨園弟子」。
entries.en: Xuanzong, himself versed in pitch, adored the fa tune and drilled three hundred Seated Bureau youths in the Pear Garden; he caught every wrong note and fixed it himself—hence "the emperor's Pear Garden disciples."
entries.literal: Emperor Xuanzong understood pitch law and dearly loved the fa tune; he chose three hundred Seated Bureau youths to teach in the Pear Garden, and if a note was wrong the emperor always noticed and corrected it—they were called "the emperor's Pear Garden disciples."

entries.zh: 宮女數百，亦為梨園弟子，居宜春北院。
entries.en: Hundreds of palace women joined as Pear Garden disciples in Yichun's north courtyard.
entries.literal: Several hundred palace women also became Pear Garden disciples and lived in the north courtyard of Yichun.

entries.zh: 梨園法部，更置小部音聲三十餘人。
entries.en: Inside the Pear Garden's fa section he added a junior troupe of some thirty players.
entries.literal: Within the Pear Garden fa section he further set up a small bureau of more than thirty musicians.

entries.zh: 帝幸驪山，楊貴妃生日，命小部張樂長生殿，因奏新曲，未有名，會南方進荔枝，因名曰《荔枝香》。
entries.en: At Mount Li on Yang Guifei's birthday the small bureau performed a new, unnamed work in the Hall of Long Life; southern lychees arrived that day, so the piece became "Lychee Fragrance."
entries.literal: When the emperor visited Mount Li on Yang Guifei's birthday he ordered the small bureau to spread music in the Hall of Long Life; as they played a new piece still without a name, lychees arrived from the south, and it was therefore named "Lychee Fragrance."

entries.zh: 帝又好羯鼓，而甯王善吹橫笛，達官大臣慕之，皆喜言音律。
entries.en: He favored the jie drum while Prince of Ning led on transverse flute; courtiers copied them and music talk became fashion.
entries.literal: The emperor also loved the jie drum, while Prince of Ning excelled at the transverse flute; high officials imitated them and all delighted in discussing pitch law.

entries.zh: 帝嘗稱：「羯鼓，八音之領袖，諸樂不可方也。」
entries.en: He once said, "The jie drum heads the eight tones—nothing else stands beside it."
entries.literal: The emperor once declared: "The jie drum is the leader of the eight sounds; no other music can compare with it."

entries.zh: 蓋本戎羯之樂，其音太蔟一均，龜茲、高昌、疏勒、天竺部皆用之，其聲焦殺，特異眾樂。
entries.en: Rooted in frontier Jie drums, it sits in the Taicu register; Kucha, Gaochang, Shule, and Tianzhu pieces all draw on it—tone biting and dry, unlike anything else in the ensemble.
entries.literal: It basically stems from Rong and Jie music; its pitch is the Taicu register; Kucha, Gaochang, Shule, and the Tianzhu bureau all use it; its sound is sharp and dry, utterly unlike other music.

entries.zh: 蓋唐自太宗、高宗作三大舞，雜用於燕樂，其他諸曲出於一時之作，雖非純雅，尚不至於淫放。
entries.en: Broadly speaking, Taizong and Gaozong gave Tang three great dances used in banquet music; other pieces were occasional works—not wholly refined, but not yet dissolute.
entries.literal: Broadly, from Taizong and Gaozong Tang composed three great dances, mingling them in banquet music; other tunes arose from momentary composition—though not purely elegant, they had not yet sunk to licentious excess.

entries.zh: 武后之禍，繼以中宗昏亂，固無足言者。
entries.en: The catastrophe of Empress Wu and Zhongzong's benighted reign scarcely need be discussed.
entries.literal: The disaster of Empress Wu, followed by Zhongzong's benighted disorder, scarcely warrants mention.

entries.zh: 玄宗為平王，有散樂一部，定韋后之難，頗有預謀者。
entries.en: As Prince of Ping, Xuanzong maintained a miscellany-music troupe and had taken no small part in planning the overthrow of Empress Wei.
entries.literal: When Xuanzong was Prince of Ping he kept a bureau of miscellany music; in settling the crisis of Empress Wei he had shared much in the plotting.

entries.zh: 及即位，命寧王主藩邸樂，以亢太常，分兩朋以角優劣。
entries.en: Once enthroned he put the Prince of Ning in charge of mansion music to rival the Grand Music Office, pitting two parties against each other in contest.
entries.literal: On his accession he charged the Prince of Ning with music at the princely mansion to rival Grand Music, dividing two factions to compete for superiority.

entries.zh: 置內教坊於蓬萊宮側，居新聲、散樂、倡優之伎，有諧謔而賜金帛朱紫者，酸棗縣尉袁楚客上疏極諫。
entries.en: He set up an Inner Music Office beside Penglai Palace for new songs, miscellany pieces, and performers; when jesters were rewarded with gold, silk, and purple robes, Yuan Chuke, lieutenant of Suanzao county, submitted a forceful memorial of remonstrance.
entries.literal: He established the Inner Music Office beside Penglai Palace to house new tunes, miscellany music, and entertainer skills; when comic banter won gifts of gold, silk, and purple rank, Yuan Chuke, county lieutenant of Suanzao, submitted a memorial vehemently remonstrating.

entries.zh: 初，帝賜第隆慶坊，坊南之地變為池，中宗常泛舟以厭其祥。
entries.en: Early on the emperor received a residence in Longqing Ward; the ground south of it became a pond, and Zhongzong would row there to dispel the ill omen.
entries.literal: At first the emperor was granted a mansion in Longqing Ward; the land south of the ward turned into a pool, and Zhongzong often went boating to suppress the omen.

entries.zh: 帝即位，作《龍池樂》，舞者十有二人，冠芙蓉冠，躡履，備用雅樂，唯無磬。
entries.en: On his accession he created "Dragon Pool Music," danced by twelve performers in lotus crowns and soft shoes to court instrumentation—everything but the stone chimes.
entries.literal: When the emperor took the throne he composed "Dragon Pool Music": twelve dancers wearing lotus crowns and treading shoes, furnished with elegant music save for no stone chimes.

entries.zh: 又作《聖壽樂》，以女子衣五色繡襟而舞之。
entries.en: He also wrote "Holy Longevity Music," performed by women in five-colored embroidered collars.
entries.literal: He also composed "Holy Longevity Music," danced by women in five-colored embroidered collars.

entries.zh: 又作《小破陣樂》，舞者被甲胄。
entries.en: He added "Little Breaking the Formation," its dancers in armor.
entries.literal: He also composed "Little Breaking the Formation Music"; the dancers wore armor.

entries.zh: 又作《光聖樂》，舞者烏冠、畫衣，以歌王跡所興。
entries.en: He also made "Radiant Sage Music," with dancers in black caps and painted robes praising the royal path he had opened.
entries.literal: He also composed "Radiant Sage Music"; dancers wore black caps and painted robes to sing of the kingly trace he had raised.

entries.zh: 又分樂為二部：堂下立奏，謂之立部伎；
entries.en: Music was then split into two troupes: pieces played standing in the hall court were the Standing Bureau;
entries.literal: He further divided music into two bureaus: performance standing below the hall was called the Standing Bureau;

entries.zh: 堂上坐奏，謂之坐部伎。
entries.en: those played seated on the dais were the Seated Bureau.
entries.literal: performance seated in the hall was called the Seated Bureau.

entries.zh: 太常閱坐部，不可教者隸立部，又不可教者，乃習雅樂。
entries.en: The Court of Sacrifices auditioned the Seated Bureau; performers who could not be trained there dropped to the Standing Bureau, and if still hopeless they were sent to elegant music.
entries.literal: The Director of Court Music reviewed the Seated Bureau; those unteachable were assigned to the Standing Bureau, and if still unteachable they studied elegant music.

entries.zh: 立部伎八：一《安舞》，二《太平樂》，三《破陣樂》，四《慶善樂》，五《大定樂》，六《上元樂》，七《聖壽樂》，八《光聖樂》。
entries.en: The Standing Bureau numbered eight works: Peace Dance, Great Peace Music, Breaking the Formation, Celebrating Goodness, Great Settlement, Upper Prime, Holy Longevity, and Radiant Sage.
entries.literal: Eight pieces of the Standing Bureau: first "Peace Dance," second "Great Peace Music," third "Breaking the Formation Music," fourth "Celebrating Goodness Music," fifth "Great Settlement Music," sixth "Upper Prime Music," seventh "Holy Longevity Music," eighth "Radiant Sage Music."

entries.zh: 《安舞》、《太平樂》，周、隋遺音也。
entries.en: "Peace Dance" and "Great Peace Music" preserve Zhou and Sui legacy.
entries.literal: "Peace Dance" and "Great Peace Music" are survivals of Zhou and Sui sound.

entries.zh: 《破陣樂》以下皆用大鼓，雜以龜茲樂，其聲震厲。
entries.en: From Breaking the Formation onward every piece used great drums with Kucha music—sound sharp enough to startle.
entries.literal: From "Breaking the Formation Music" downward all used great drums mixed with Kucha music; the sound was thunderous and fierce.

entries.zh: 《大定樂》又加金鉦。
entries.en: "Great Settlement Music" layered in golden cymbals.
entries.literal: "Great Settlement Music" added golden cymbals as well.

entries.zh: 《慶善舞》顓用西涼樂，聲頗閒雅。
entries.en: "Celebrating Goodness Dance" relied wholly on Western Liang music and sounded notably calm and elegant.
entries.literal: "Celebrating Goodness Dance" exclusively used Western Liang music; the sound was quite leisurely and refined.

entries.zh: 每享郊廟，則《破陣》、《上元》、《慶善》三舞皆用之。
entries.en: At every suburban and temple sacrifice the three dances Breaking the Formation, Upper Prime, and Celebrating Goodness were performed.
entries.literal: Whenever suburban and ancestral temples were feasted, the three dances "Breaking the Formation," "Upper Prime," and "Celebrating Goodness" were all used.

entries.zh: 坐部伎六：一《燕樂》，二《長壽樂》，三《天授樂》，四《鳥歌萬歲樂》，五《龍池樂》，六《小破陣樂》。
entries.en: The Seated Bureau had six: Banquet Music, Longevity Music, Heaven-Bestowed Music, Bird Song of Ten Thousand Years, Dragon Pool, and Little Breaking the Formation.
entries.literal: Six pieces of the Seated Bureau: first "Banquet Music," second "Longevity Music," third "Heaven-Bestowed Music," fourth "Bird Song of Ten Thousand Years Music," fifth "Dragon Pool Music," sixth "Little Breaking the Formation Music."

entries.zh: 《天授》、《鳥歌》，皆武后作也。
entries.en: Heaven-Bestowed and Bird Song both came from Empress Wu.
entries.literal: "Heaven-Bestowed" and "Bird Song" were both composed by Empress Wu.

entries.zh: 天授，年名。
entries.en: Heaven-Bestowed was her reign era name.
entries.literal: Heaven-Bestowed is a reign title.

entries.zh: 鳥歌者，有鳥能人言萬歲，因以制樂。
entries.en: Bird Song arose when a bird was said to cry "ten thousand years," inspiring the piece.
entries.literal: As for Bird Song: a bird could speak "ten thousand years," and music was composed on that account.

entries.zh: 自《長壽樂》以下，用龜茲舞，唯《龍池樂》則否。
entries.en: From Longevity Music down the Kucha dance style was used—Dragon Pool alone excepted.
entries.literal: From "Longevity Music" downward Kucha dance was used; only "Dragon Pool Music" did not.

entries.zh: 中宗時，百濟樂工人亡散，岐王為太常卿，復奏置之，然音伎多闕。
entries.en: Under Zhongzong Baekje players dispersed; Prince of Qi, as Court Director, restored the troupe, but much technique was gone.
entries.literal: In Zhongzong's time Baekje musicians scattered and were lost; Prince of Qi as Court Director memorialized to restore and install them, yet most musical skills were missing.

entries.zh: 舞者二人，紫大袖裙襦、章甫冠、衣履。
entries.en: Two dancers wore purple wide-sleeved jackets and skirts with zhangfu caps and full dress.
entries.literal: Two dancers wore purple great-sleeved jackets and skirts, zhangfu caps, and robes and shoes.

entries.zh: 樂有箏、笛、桃皮觱篥、箜篌、歌而已。
entries.en: Instrumentation was limited to zheng, flute, peach-bark bili, konghou, and voice.
entries.literal: The music had only zheng, di, peach-bark bili, konghou, and song.

entries.zh: 玄宗又嘗以馬百匹，盛飾分左右，施三重榻，舞《傾杯》數十曲，壯士舉榻，馬不動。
entries.en: He once arrayed a hundred richly caparisoned horses with triple couches and danced dozens of Tipping the Cup numbers while brawny men heaved the couches without budging the animals.
entries.literal: Xuanzong also once took a hundred horses lavishly caparisoned left and right, set triple couches, and danced dozens of "Tipping the Cup" pieces; strong men lifted the couches yet the horses did not stir.

entries.zh: 樂工少年姿秀者十數人，衣黃衫、文玉帶，立左右。
entries.en: A dozen-odd handsome young players in yellow jackets and patterned jade belts flanked the scene.
entries.literal: More than a dozen youthful, handsome musicians wore yellow jackets and patterned jade belts and stood left and right.

entries.zh: 每千秋節，舞於勤政樓下，後賜宴設酺，亦會勤政樓。
entries.en: Each Thousand Autumns Festival they danced beneath the Diligence-in-Government Tower; later court feasts with public wine met there too.
entries.literal: Every Thousand Autumns Festival they danced below the Diligence-in-Government Tower; later banquets with communal wine also gathered at that tower.

entries.zh: 其日未明，金吾引駕騎，北衙四軍陳仗，列旗幟，被金甲、短後繡袍。
entries.en: Before dawn the Golden Crow guard led the cavalcade; four northern-yard armies formed ranks in golden armor and short embroidered surcoats.
entries.literal: Before dawn that day the Golden Crow guard led the imperial escort; the four northern-yard armies deployed arms, lined banners and flags, wore golden armor and short embroidered rear-guards.

entries.zh: 太常卿引雅樂，每部數十人，間以胡夷之技。
entries.en: The Court Director led elegant music—dozens per section—punctuated by foreign acts.
entries.literal: The Court Director led elegant music, several dozen per section, interspersed with barbarian skills.

entries.zh: 內閑廄使引戲馬，五坊使引象、犀，入場拜舞。
entries.en: The Inner Stud led performing horses; the Five Paddocks led elephants and rhinos to enter and bow in dance.
entries.literal: The Inner Stud envoy led trick horses; the Five Paddocks envoy led elephants and rhinoceroses to enter the ground and bow in dance.

entries.zh: 宮人數百衣錦繡衣，出帷中，擊雷鼓，奏《小破陣樂》，歲以為常。
entries.en: Hundreds of palace women in brocade slipped from behind curtains, beat thunder drums, and played Little Breaking the Formation—an annual ritual.
entries.literal: Several hundred palace women in brocade robes emerged from within the curtain, struck thunder drums, and performed "Little Breaking the Formation Music"—year after year as custom.

entries.zh: 千秋節者，玄宗以八月五日生，因以其日名節，而君臣共為荒樂，當時流俗多傳其事以為盛。
entries.en: The Thousand Autumns Festival marked Xuanzong's birthday on the eighth month's fifth day; court and emperor abandoned themselves to revelry, and contemporaries trumpeted the spectacle.
entries.literal: The Thousand Autumns Festival: Xuanzong was born on the fifth day of the eighth month, and therefore named the festival for that day; ruler and ministers together indulged in reckless music, and popular custom widely transmitted the affair as splendor.

entries.zh: 其後巨盜起，陷兩京，自此天下用兵不息，而離宮苑囿遂以荒堙，獨其餘聲遺曲傳人間，聞者為之悲涼感動。
entries.en: Then rebellion took both capitals; war never lifted, pleasure parks rotted away, and only fragments of music wandered among common folk, stirring grief in whoever heard them.
entries.literal: Later a great bandit arose and seized the two capitals; from then on warfare in the realm never ceased, while detached palaces and parks fell to ruin—only stray sounds and surviving tunes passed among the people, and hearers were moved to sorrow and chill.

entries.zh: 蓋其事適足為戒，而不足考法，故不復著其詳。
entries.en: The episode warns more than it instructs, so the account stops short of full detail.
entries.literal: Those affairs are just enough to serve as warning and not enough to take as model; therefore the details are not recorded further.

entries.zh: 自肅宗以後，皆以生日為節，而德宗不立節，然止於群臣稱觴上壽而已。
entries.en: After Suzong emperors marked birthdays as holidays; Dezong refused the practice, limiting celebration to ministers' toast for long life.
entries.literal: From Suzong onward birthdays became festivals, yet Dezong established no festival—only stopping at ministers raising cups and offering longevity wishes.

entries.zh: 開元二十四年，升胡部於堂上。
entries.en: Kaiyuan 24 raised the foreign bureau to hall performance.
entries.literal: In the twenty-fourth year of Kaiyuan the barbarian bureau was elevated to the hall.

entries.zh: 而天寶樂曲，皆以邊地名，若《涼州》、《伊州》、《甘州》之類。
entries.en: By the Tianbao reign most new tunes bore border place-names—Liangzhou, Yizhou, Ganzhou, and the like.
entries.literal: Yet Tianbao era pieces mostly took frontier place-names, such as "Liangzhou," "Yizhou," and "Ganzhou."

entries.zh: 後又詔道調、法曲與胡部新聲合作。
entries.en: An edict then fused Daodiao, fa music, and fresh barbarian melodies.
entries.literal: Later an edict ordered Daodiao, fa tunes, and new barbarian sounds to be combined.

entries.zh: 明年，安祿山反，涼州、伊州、甘州皆陷吐蕃。
entries.en: The following year An Lushan rose; Liangzhou, Yizhou, and Ganzhou were lost to Tibet.
entries.literal: The next year An Lushan rebelled; Liangzhou, Yizhou, and Ganzhou all fell to Tibet.

entries.zh: 是時，民間以帝自潞州還京師，舉兵夜半誅韋皇后，制《夜半樂》、《還京樂》二曲。
entries.en: Popular musicians then wrote "Midnight Music" and "Returning to the Capital," commemorating his midnight march from Luzhou to kill Empress Wei.
entries.literal: At that time the people, because the emperor had returned from Luzhou to the capital at midnight and raised troops to execute Empress Wei, composed the two tunes "Midnight Music" and "Returning to the Capital Music."

entries.zh: 帝又作《文成曲》，與《小破陣樂》更奏之。
entries.en: He also wrote "Wencheng Tune," paired in rotation with Little Breaking the Formation.
entries.literal: The emperor also composed "Wencheng Tune" and alternated it with "Little Breaking the Formation Music."

entries.zh: 其後，河西節度使楊敬忠獻《霓裳羽衣曲》十二遍，凡曲終必遽，唯《霓裳羽衣曲》將畢，引聲益緩。
entries.en: Later Yang Jingzhong of Hexi presented the Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe in twelve passes; most suites rushed their endings, but this one deliberately slowed as it finished.
entries.literal: Later Hexi Military Commissioner Yang Jingzhong presented the "Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe" in twelve repetitions; whenever a piece ended it always hurried, but as the "Rainbow Skirt" neared its close the leading sound grew ever slower.

entries.zh: 帝方浸喜神仙之事，詔道士司馬承禎制《玄真道曲》，茅山道士李會元制《大羅天曲》，工部侍郎賀知章制《紫清上聖道曲》。
entries.en: As his taste turned toward immortals he commissioned Sima Chengzhen's "Mysterious Truth Dao Tune," Li Huiyuan of Maoshan's "Great Luo Heaven Tune," and He Zhizhang's "Purple Clarity Supreme Sage Dao Tune."
entries.literal: The emperor was then increasingly fond of immortal matters; he ordered Daoist priest Sima Chengzhen to compose "Mysterious Truth Dao Tune," Maoshan priest Li Huiyuan to compose "Great Luo Heaven Tune," and Ministry Vice Minister He Zhizhang to compose "Purple Clarity Supreme Sage Dao Tune."

entries.zh: 太清宮成，太常卿韋縚制《景雲》、《九真》、《紫極》、《小長壽》、《承天》、《順天樂》六曲，又制商調《君臣相遇樂》曲。
entries.en: At the Supreme Clarity Palace's completion Wei Tao, Director of Court Music, offered six pieces—Jingyun, Nine Perfections, Purple Pole, Little Longevity, Receiving Heaven, Following Heaven—and a shang-mode suite, Ruler and Minister Meeting in Joy.
entries.literal: When the Supreme Clarity Palace was completed, Court Director Wei Tao composed six tunes—"Jingyun," "Nine Perfections," "Purple Pole," "Little Longevity," "Receiving Heaven," and "Following Heaven Music"—and also composed the shang-mode tune "Ruler and Minister Meeting in Joy."

entries.zh: 自高祖初入長安，開大丞相府，下令置生員，自京師至於州縣皆有數。
entries.en: When Gaozu first entered Chang'an and opened the Grand Chancellor's Office, he ordered student quotas established at every level from the capital down to prefectures and counties.
entries.literal: From the time Gaozu first entered Chang'an and opened the Grand Chancellor's Office, he issued orders to establish student quotas, with fixed numbers from the capital down to prefectures and counties.

entries.zh: 既即位，又詔秘書外省別立小學，以教宗室子孫及功臣子弟。
entries.en: After his enthronement, he also ordered a separate elementary school outside the Secretariat to educate imperial clan descendants and sons of meritorious officials.
entries.literal: After he took the throne, he also ordered a separate elementary school established outside the Secretariat to teach imperial clan descendants and sons of meritorious officials.

entries.zh: 其後又詔諸州明經、秀才、俊士、進士明于理體為鄉里稱者，縣考試，州長重覆，歲隨方物入貢；
entries.en: He later ordered that throughout the empire, candidates in Mingjing, Xiucai, Junshi, and Jinshi who showed mastery of principle and were acclaimed locally should be examined by their county, re-examined by the prefect, and sent annually to court with local tribute;
entries.literal: Later he also ordered that in all prefectures those in Mingjing, Xiucai, Junshi, and Jinshi who were clear in principle and structure and acclaimed in their districts should be examined by the county, re-examined by the prefect, and each year sent in tribute with local products;

entries.zh: 吏民子弟學藝者，皆送於京學，為設考課之法。
entries.en: sons of officials and commoners studying the arts were all sent to capital schools, and examination regulations were established for them.
entries.literal: sons of officials and commoners who studied arts were all sent to the capital schools, for which examination regulations were established.

entries.zh: 州、縣、鄉皆置學焉。
entries.en: Schools were established at the prefectural, county, and district levels.
entries.literal: Schools were established in prefectures, counties, and districts alike.

entries.zh: 及太宗即位，益崇儒術。
entries.en: When Taizong came to the throne, he gave even greater prominence to Confucian learning.
entries.literal: When Taizong took the throne, he further honored Confucian learning.

entries.zh: 乃于門下別置弘文館，又增置書、律學，進士加讀經、史一部。
entries.en: He established the Hongwen Academy under the Secretariat, added Writing and Law schools, and required Jinshi candidates to study an additional classic or historical work.
entries.literal: He then separately established the Hongwen Academy under the Secretariat, also added Writing and Law schools, and required Jinshi candidates to read an additional classic or history.

entries.zh: 十三年，東宮置崇文館。
entries.en: In his thirteenth year, the Eastern Palace established the Chongwen Academy.
entries.literal: In the thirteenth year, the Eastern Palace established the Chongwen Academy.

entries.zh: 自天下初定，增築學舍至千二百區，雖七營飛騎，亦置生，遣博士為授經。
entries.en: After the empire was pacified, school buildings increased to twelve hundred wards. Even the seven camps of flying cavalry enrolled students and were assigned erudites to teach the classics.
entries.literal: From the time the realm was first pacified, school buildings were increased to twelve hundred wards; even the seven camps of flying cavalry had students placed, with erudites dispatched to lecture on the classics.

entries.zh: 四夷若高麗、百濟、新羅、高昌、吐蕃，相繼遣子弟入學，遂至八千餘人。
entries.en: Foreign states including Koguryo, Paekche, Silla, Gaochang, and Tibet successively sent princes and sons to study, until enrollment exceeded eight thousand.
entries.literal: Barbarians of the four directions such as Koguryo, Paekche, Silla, Gaochang, and Tibet sent sons in succession to study, until there were more than eight thousand persons.

entries.zh: 武后之亂，改易舊制頗多。
entries.en: During Empress Wu's reign, many longstanding institutions were altered.
entries.literal: During the turmoil of Empress Wu, many old institutions were changed.

entries.zh: 中宗反正，詔宗室三等以下、五等以上未出身，願宿衛及任國子生，聽之。
entries.en: After Zhongzong's restoration, he decreed that imperial clansmen of the third rank and below and fifth rank and above who had not yet received office might serve in the palace guard or enroll as National University students if they wished.
entries.literal: When Zhongzong restored the proper order, he decreed that imperial clansmen of the third rank and below and fifth rank and above who had not yet received appointment, if they wished to serve in the palace guard or take office as National University students, were permitted to do so.

entries.zh: 其家居業成而堪貢者，宗正寺試，送監舉如常法。
entries.en: Clansmen who completed their studies at home and were fit for presentation were examined by the Imperial Clan Court and forwarded to the directorate by the usual procedure.
entries.literal: Those who at home completed their studies and were fit for tribute presentation were examined by the Imperial Clan Court and sent to the directorate for presentation by the usual method.

entries.zh: 三衛番下日，願入學者，聽附國子學、太學及律館習業。
entries.en: When guards of the Three Guards rotated off duty, those who wished to study were permitted to enroll in the National University, Great Academy, or Law School.
entries.literal: On days when the Three Guards rotated off duty, those who wished to enter study were permitted to attach to the National University, Great Academy, and Law School for their studies.

entries.zh: 蕃王及可汗子孫願入學者，附國子學讀書。
entries.en: Sons and grandsons of foreign kings and khans who wished to study were enrolled in the National University.
entries.literal: Sons and grandsons of barbarian kings and khans who wished to enter study attached to the National University for reading.

entries.zh: 玄宗開元五年，始令鄉貢明經、進士見訖，國子監謁先師，學官開講問義，有司為具食，清資五品以上官及朝集使皆往閱禮焉。
entries.en: In 717, Xuanzong ordered that after their audience, local-tribute Mingjing and Jinshi candidates visit the Confucian temple at the Directorate of Education, where instructors lectured and discussed the classics. The government provided a feast, and fifth-rank officials and assembly envoys attended to observe the rites.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Kaiyuan under Xuanzong, it was first ordered that after local-tribute Mingjing and Jinshi candidates had completed their audience, they should visit the sage at the Directorate of Education; academic officials opened lectures and questioned on principles; the offices provided food; officials of pure appointment of the fifth rank and above and assembly envoys all went to observe the ceremony.

entries.zh: 七年，又令弘文、崇文、國子生季一朝參。
entries.en: In 719, he also required Hongwen, Chongwen, and National University students to attend court once each season.
entries.literal: In the seventh year, it was further ordered that Hongwen, Chongwen, and National University students attend court once each season.

entries.zh: 及注《老子道德經》成，詔天下家藏其書，貢舉人滅《尚書》、《論語》策，而加試《老子》。
entries.en: When Xuanzong finished his commentary on the Laozi, he ordered every household to keep a copy. Examination candidates faced fewer policy questions on the Documents and Analects, and the Laozi was added to the test.
entries.literal: When the commentary on the Laozi's Classic of the Way and Virtue was completed, an edict ordered every household in the realm to keep a copy; tribute candidates had their policy questions on the Documents and Analects reduced, and the Laozi was added to the examination.

entries.zh: 又敕州縣學生年二十五以下、八品子若庶人二十一以下通一經及未通經而聰悟有文辭、史學者，入四門學為俊士。
entries.en: He further decreed that prefectural and county students under twenty-five, sons of eighth-rank officials or commoners under twenty-one who had mastered one classic—or who showed literary or historical talent even without completing a classic—could enter the Four Gates Academy as Junshi.
entries.literal: It was further ordered that prefectural and county students twenty-five and below, sons of eighth-rank officials or commoners twenty-one and below who had mastered one classic, or who had not mastered a classic but were intelligent with literary skill or historical learning, should enter the Four Gates Academy as Junshi.

entries.zh: 即諸州貢舉省試不第，願入學者亦聽。
entries.en: Candidates from the provinces who failed the capital examination but wished to continue studying were also permitted to enroll.
entries.literal: That is, those from all prefectures who failed the provincial examination for tribute presentation but wished to enter study were also permitted.

entries.zh: 二十四年，考功員外郎李昂為舉人詆訶，帝以員外郎望輕，遂移貢舉於禮部，以侍郎主之。
entries.en: In 736, Vice-Director Li Ang was publicly insulted by candidates. The emperor considered the vice-director's rank too low and transferred the examinations to the Ministry of Rites, to be chaired by a vice-minister.
entries.literal: In the twenty-fourth year, Vice-Director of Personnel Li Ang was reviled by candidates; the emperor considered the vice-director's standing too light, and therefore moved tribute presentation examinations to the Ministry of Rites, with a vice-minister presiding.

entries.zh: 禮部選士自此始。
entries.en: From this point the Ministry of Rites took charge of selecting scholars.
entries.literal: The Ministry of Rites' selection of scholars began from this point.

entries.zh: 二十九年，始置崇玄學，習《老子》、《莊子》、《文子》、《列子》，亦曰道舉。
entries.en: In 741, the Chongxuan School was established to study the Laozi, Zhuangzi, Wenzi, and Liezi. It was also known as the Daoist recommendation examination.
entries.literal: In the twenty-ninth year, the Chongxuan School was first established to study the Laozi, Zhuangzi, Wenzi, and Liezi—it was also called Daoist recommendation.

entries.zh: 其生，京、都各百人，諸州無常員。
entries.en: Enrollment was one hundred each in Chang'an and Luoyang; prefectures had no fixed quotas.
entries.literal: Its students: one hundred each in the capital and eastern capital; prefectures had no fixed quotas.

entries.zh: 官秩、廕第同國子，舉送、課試如明經。
entries.en: Official ranks, hereditary privileges, presentation procedures, and examinations followed the same rules as the National University and Mingjing candidates.
entries.literal: Official rank, hereditary privilege, and presentation and examination followed the same rules as the National University and Mingjing.

entries.zh: 天寶九載，置廣文館于國學，以領生徒為進士者。
entries.en: In 750, the Guangwen Academy was established within the National University to supervise students preparing for the Jinshi examination.
entries.literal: In the ninth year of Tianbao, the Guangwen Academy was established within the National University to oversee students who were Jinshi candidates.

entries.zh: 舉人舊重兩監，後世祿者以京兆、同、華為榮，而不入學。
entries.en: Candidates had once prized enrollment in the two directorates of education; by later times, those seeking office took pride in qualifying through Jingzhao, Tongzhou, or Huazhou and no longer entered the schools at all.
entries.literal: Candidates of old prized the two directorates; in later times those seeking salary took pride in Jingzhao, Tong, and Hua, and did not enter the schools.

entries.zh: 十二載，乃敕天下罷鄉貢，舉人不由國子及郡、縣學者，勿舉送。
entries.en: In 753, an edict abolished local tribute examinations empire-wide; candidates who had not passed through the National University or prefectural and county schools were not to be forwarded for examination.
entries.literal: In the twelfth year, an edict abolished local tribute throughout the realm; candidates who had not come through the National University or prefectural and county schools were not to be presented.

entries.zh: 是歲，道舉停《老子》，加《周易》。
entries.en: That same year the Daoist recommendation examination dropped the Laozi and added the Book of Changes.
entries.literal: That year, the Daoist examination dropped the Laozi and added the Book of Changes.

entries.zh: 十四載，復鄉貢。
entries.en: In 755, local tribute examinations were restored.
entries.literal: In the fourteenth year, local tribute was restored.

entries.zh: 「夏之政忠，商之政敬，周之政文，然則文與忠敬皆統人行。
entries.en: "Xia government was marked by sincerity, Shang by reverence, Zhou by culture—yet culture, sincerity, and reverence alike govern human conduct.
entries.literal: "The government of Xia was marked by sincerity, that of Shang by reverence, that of Zhou by culture—thus culture together with sincerity and reverence all govern human conduct.

entries.zh: 且諡號述行，莫美于文，文興則忠敬存焉。
entries.en: Posthumous titles describe a person's conduct, and none is finer than "Cultured"; when culture flourishes, sincerity and reverence endure.
entries.literal: Moreover, posthumous titles describe conduct, and none is more beautiful than culture; when culture flourishes, sincerity and reverence are preserved therein.

entries.zh: 故前代以文取士，本文行也，由辭觀行，則及辭焉。
entries.en: Earlier dynasties selected officials by literary accomplishment because writing reveals character; to judge conduct through writing is to reach the writing itself.
entries.literal: Therefore earlier ages took scholars by literary accomplishment—this was rooted in conduct and character; observing conduct through literary expression reaches even to the expression itself.

entries.zh: 宣父稱顏子「不遷怒，不貳過」，謂之「好學」。
entries.en: Confucius praised Yan Hui for "never transferring anger, never repeating a fault," and called this true love of learning.
entries.literal: The Master praised Yan Hui for "not transferring anger, not repeating faults," calling this "fondness for learning."

entries.zh: 今試學者以帖字為精通，不窮旨義，豈能知遷怒、貳過之道乎？
entries.en: Today we test students on fill-in passages as if that were mastery, without probing deeper meaning—how can they grasp the way of not transferring anger or repeating faults?
entries.literal: Today examinees are tested on fill-in characters as mastery, without exhausting principles and meanings—how can they know the way of not transferring anger or repeating faults?

entries.zh: 考文者以聲病為是非，豈能知移風易俗化天下乎？
entries.en: Examiners judge compositions by tonal patterns—how can they know how to transform customs and civilize the realm?
entries.literal: Those who examine literary works take tonal patterns as the standard of right and wrong—how can they know transforming customs and changing popular ways to civilize all under Heaven?

entries.zh: 是以上失其源，下襲其流，先王之道莫能行也。
entries.en: Thus those above have lost the source and those below merely follow the current—the way of the ancient kings can no longer be practiced.
entries.literal: Thus above loses the source and below inherits the current; the way of the former kings can no longer be practiced.

entries.zh: 夫先王之道消，則小人之道長，亂臣賊子由是生焉！
entries.en: When the way of the ancient kings fades, the way of petty men flourishes—and rebellious ministers and wicked sons arise from it!
entries.literal: When the way of the former kings fades, the way of petty men grows long—rebellious ministers and wicked sons arise from this!

entries.zh: 今取士試之小道，而不以遠大，是猶以蝸蚓之餌垂海，而望吞舟之魚，不亦難乎？
entries.en: To select officials by petty tests rather than great purpose is like dangling worm bait over the sea and hoping to catch a leviathan—is it not futile?
entries.literal: Now in taking scholars one tests petty paths and not the far-reaching and great—this is like dangling snail-and-worm bait over the sea and hoping for fish that swallow boats—is it not difficult?

entries.zh: 所以食垂餌者皆小魚，就科目者皆小藝。
entries.en: Only small fish take dangling bait; only petty skills win examination degrees.
entries.literal: Those that eat dangling bait are all small fish; those who pursue examination categories are all petty arts.

entries.zh: 且夏有天下四百載，禹之道喪而商始興；
entries.en: Xia ruled for four hundred years before Yu's way was lost and Shang rose;
entries.literal: Moreover, Xia held the realm for four hundred years; Yu's way was lost and Shang then rose;

entries.zh: 商有天下六百祀，湯之法棄而周始興；
entries.en: Shang ruled for six hundred years before Tang's laws were abandoned and Zhou rose;
entries.literal: Shang held the realm for six hundred reign-years; Tang's laws were abandoned and Zhou then rose;

entries.zh: 周有天下八百年，文、武之政廢而秦始並焉。
entries.en: Zhou ruled for eight hundred years before the government of King Wen and King Wu was abandoned and Qin united the realm.
entries.literal: Zhou held the realm for eight hundred years; the government of Wen and Wu was abandoned and Qin then united it.

entries.zh: 三代之選士任賢，皆考實行，是以風俗淳一，運祚長遠。
entries.en: The Three Dynasties selected officials by examining actual conduct; customs remained pure and their rule endured.
entries.literal: The Three Dynasties in selecting scholars and appointing the worthy all examined actual conduct; thus customs were pure and unified and fortune endured far and long.

entries.zh: 漢興，監其然，尊儒術，尚名節，雖近戚竊位，強臣擅權，弱主外立，母后專政，而亦能終彼四百，豈非學行之效邪？
entries.en: When Han arose, it observed this pattern, honored Confucian learning, and prized integrity. Though kinsmen seized office, powerful ministers monopolized authority, weak rulers were installed from outside, and empress dowagers dominated government, Han still endured four hundred years—is this not the fruit of learning and conduct?
entries.literal: When Han arose, it observed this, honored Confucian learning, and esteemed reputation and integrity; though close kin usurped posts, powerful ministers monopolized authority, weak rulers were installed from outside, and empress dowagers held government—yet it could still complete those four hundred years—is this not the effect of learning and conduct?

entries.zh: 魏、晉以來，專尚浮侈，德義不修，故子孫速顛，享國不永也。
entries.en: From Wei and Jin onward, rulers prized superficial luxury and neglected virtue and righteousness; their dynasties fell swiftly and did not endure.
entries.literal: From Wei and Jin onward, they devoted themselves only to superficial luxury and did not cultivate virtue and righteousness; thus their descendants quickly fell and their enjoyment of the realm was not long.

entries.zh: 今綰所請，實為正論。
entries.en: Yang Wan's proposal is fundamentally sound.
entries.literal: What Wan now requests is truly correct doctrine.

entries.zh: 然自晉室之亂，南北分裂，人多僑處，必欲復古鄉舉裏選，竊恐未盡。
entries.en: Yet since the Jin collapse and the north-south division, many people have lived far from their native places; a full restoration of ancient village recommendation and district selection may not yet be practicable.
entries.literal: Yet since the disorder of the Jin house, north and south were divided and many people lived as sojourners; if one must restore the ancient village recommendation and district selection, I fear privately that it may not be fully feasible.

entries.zh: 請兼廣學校，以明訓誘。
entries.en: I propose instead expanding the schools to spread instruction and moral guidance.
entries.literal: I request also expanding the schools to make instruction clear and guide by teaching.

entries.zh: 雖京師州縣皆有小學，兵革之後，生徒流離，儒臣、師氏，祿廩無向。
entries.en: Although the capital and prefectures all maintained elementary schools, after the wars students scattered and Confucian teachers had no reliable salaries.
entries.literal: Although the capital and prefectures and counties all had elementary schools, after the armies and weapons, student disciples were scattered, Confucian officials and teachers had no direction for salary and grain rations.

entries.zh: 請增博士員，厚其稟稍，選通儒碩生，間居其職。
entries.en: Increase the number of erudites, raise their stipends, and appoint broadly learned eminent scholars to these posts.
entries.literal: I request increasing the number of erudites, enriching their stipends, and selecting broadly learned eminent scholars to fill the posts in turn.

entries.zh: 十道大郡，置太學館，遣博士出外，兼領郡官，以教生徒。
entries.en: In the major prefectures of the ten circuits, establish Imperial University hostels, dispatch erudites to serve concurrently as prefectural officials, and charge them with instructing students.
entries.literal: In the great prefectures of the ten circuits, establish Imperial University hostels, send erudites outward, and have them concurrently hold prefectural office to instruct student disciples.

entries.zh: 保桑梓者，鄉里舉焉；
entries.en: Those who remain in their native districts should be recommended by village and township;
entries.literal: Those who preserve their native place should be recommended by village and district;

entries.zh: 在流寓者，庠序推焉。
entries.en: those living abroad should be nominated by local schools.
entries.literal: those living as sojourners should be promoted by the local schools.

entries.zh: 朝而行之，夕見其利。」
entries.en: Adopt this in the morning and see its benefit by evening."
entries.literal: Implement it in the morning and by evening see its benefit."

entries.zh: 唐制，取士之科，多因隋舊，然其大要有三。
entries.en: Tang rules for selecting officials drew heavily on Sui practice, but in essence there were three main paths.
entries.literal: Under Tang institutions, the categories for recruiting scholars largely followed Sui precedents, yet in broad outline there were three.

entries.zh: 由學館者曰生徒，由州縣者曰鄉貢，皆升於有司而進退之。
entries.en: Candidates from state schools were called "student disciples"; those recommended by prefectures and counties were called "local tribute." Both were forwarded to the responsible offices, which decided who advanced and who did not.
entries.literal: Those coming through academies were called student disciples; those coming through prefectures and counties were called local tribute; all were advanced to the competent offices, which promoted or rejected them.

entries.zh: 其科之目，有秀才，有明經，有俊士，有進士，有明法，有明字，有明算，有一史，有三史，有開元禮，有道舉，有童子。
entries.en: Examination categories included Xiucai (literary talent), Mingjing (classics), Junshi (outstanding scholars), Jinshi (presented scholars), Mingfa (law), Mingzi (writing), Mingsuan (mathematics), one-history and three-history examinations, Kaiyuan Rites, Daoist recommendation, and Tongzi (child prodigy).
entries.literal: The categories of examinations included Xiucai, Mingjing, Junshi, Jinshi, Mingfa, Mingzi, Mingsuan, one-history, three-history, Kaiyuan Rites, Daoist recommendation, and Tongzi.

entries.zh: 而明經之別，有五經，有三經，有二經，有學究一經，有三禮，有三傳，有史科。
entries.en: Mingjing itself was subdivided into five-classics, three-classics, two-classics, single-classic specialized study, Three Rites, Three Commentaries, and history examinations.
entries.literal: The subdivisions of Mingjing were Five Classics, Three Classics, Two Classics, one-classic specialized study, Three Rites, Three Commentaries, and history examinations.

entries.zh: 此歲舉之常選也。
entries.en: These were the routine annual examinations.
entries.literal: These were the regular selections held each year.

entries.zh: 其天子自詔者曰制舉，所以待非常之才焉。
entries.en: Examinations specially proclaimed by the emperor were called "decree examinations," reserved for recruiting exceptional talent.
entries.literal: Those personally summoned by edict of the Son of Heaven were called decree examinations, by which extraordinary talent was recruited.

entries.zh: 中宗時，韋後及太平、安樂公主等用事，於側門降墨敕斜封授官，號「斜封官」，凡數千員。
entries.en: Under Zhongzong, Empress Wei and the Princesses Taiping and Anle ruled through side-gate edicts with slanted seals, creating thousands of "slanted-seal" appointees.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Zhongzong, Empress Wei and the Princesses of Peace and of Peaceful Joy held power; at the side gate they issued ink edicts with slanted seals to grant office—called "slanted-seal officials"—several thousand posts in all.

entries.zh: 內外盈溢，無聽事以居，當時謂之「三無坐處」，言宰相、御史及員外郎也。
entries.en: Offices overflowed so that chancellors, censors, and aides had nowhere to sit—the age called it "three offices with no seat."
entries.literal: Inside and outside overflowed; there were no offices to sit in. The age called it "three offices with nowhere to sit," meaning chancellors, censors, and aides.

entries.zh: 又以鄭愔為侍郎，大納貨賂，選人留者甚眾，至逆用三年員闕，而綱紀大潰。
entries.en: Zheng Yin as vice minister took huge bribes, detained masses of candidates, and even filled posts three years in advance, collapsing the system.
entries.literal: Zheng Yin was again made vice minister, greatly accepting bribes; candidates detained were very numerous, even using three years of vacant posts in reverse, and discipline greatly collapsed.

entries.zh: 韋氏敗，始以宋璟為吏部尚書，李乂、盧從願為侍郎，姚元之為兵部尚書，陸象先、盧懷慎為侍郎，悉奏罷斜封官，量闕留人，雖資高考深，非才實者不取。
entries.en: After the Wei clan's fall, Song Jing, Li Yi, Lu Congyuan, Yao Yuanzhi, Lu Xiangxian, and Lu Huaishen abolished slanted-seal posts, matched vacancies to candidates, and refused men of high seniority but no real ability.
entries.literal: When the Wei clan fell, Song Jing was first made Minister of Personnel, Li Yi and Lu Congyuan vice ministers, Yao Yuanzhi Minister of War, Lu Xiangxian and Lu Huaishen vice ministers; all memorialized to abolish slanted-seal officials, measured vacancies and retained men; though seniority was high and examination deep, those without real talent were not taken.

entries.zh: 初，尚書銓掌七品以上選，侍郎銓掌八品以下選。
entries.en: Originally the minister handled selection for seventh rank and above, vice ministers for eighth rank and below.
entries.literal: At first the minister evaluated selection for seventh rank and above; vice ministers evaluated eighth rank and below.

entries.zh: 至是，通其品而掌焉。
entries.en: Now they handled all ranks together.
entries.literal: At this point ranks were unified and they managed all.

entries.zh: 未幾，璟、元之等罷，殿中侍御史崔涖、太子中允薛昭希太平公主意，上言：「罷斜封官，人失其所，而怨積於下，必有非常之變。」
entries.en: Soon Song and Yao were dismissed; Cui Li and Xue Zhao, courting Princess Taiping, warned: "Abolishing slanted-seal posts leaves men displaced, resentment builds below, and disaster will follow."
entries.literal: Before long Jing, Yuanzhi, and others were dismissed; Palace Censor Cui Li and Crown Prince Attendant Xue Zhao, pleasing Princess Taiping, submitted: "Abolishing slanted-seal officials, men lose their place, resentment accumulates below, and there will surely be extraordinary change."

entries.zh: 乃下詔盡復斜封別敕官。
entries.en: An edict then fully restored slanted-seal and special-edict appointments.
entries.literal: An edict was then issued fully restoring slanted-seal and special-edict officials.

entries.zh: 玄宗即位，厲精為治。
entries.en: When Xuanzong took the throne, he threw himself into reform.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xuanzong took the throne, he applied himself diligently to governance.

entries.zh: 左拾遺內供奉張九齡上疏言：「縣令、刺史，陛下所與共理，尤親於民者也。
entries.en: Zhang Jiuling submitted: "Magistrates and prefects are Your Majesty's partners in governing the people.
entries.literal: Left Reminder and Inner Attendant Zhang Jiuling submitted: "Magistrates and prefects are those Your Majesty governs with—especially close to the people.

entries.zh: 今京官出外，乃反以為斥逐，非少重其選不可。」
entries.en: Yet capital officials treat local posts as exile; their selection must be taken more seriously."
entries.literal: Now when capital officials go out, it is instead taken as banishment; selection for these posts cannot but be made weightier."

entries.zh: 又曰：「古者或遙聞辟召，或一見任之，是以士脩名行，而流品不雜。
entries.en: He added: "In antiquity men were recruited by reputation or appointed at first meeting, so scholars cultivated conduct and ranks stayed pure.
entries.literal: He also said: "In antiquity men were sometimes summoned from afar on reputation, sometimes appointed at a single meeting; thus scholars cultivated conduct and rank was not mixed.

entries.zh: 今吏部始造簿書，以備遺忘，而反求精於案牘，不急人才，何異遺劍中流，而刻舟以記。」
entries.en: Now the Ministry keeps ledgers against forgetfulness yet prizes paperwork over talent—like marking the boat after losing a sword in the river."
entries.literal: Now the Ministry of Personnel first makes ledgers to guard against forgetting, yet instead seeks precision in documents, not urgently seeking talent—how is this different from losing a sword in midstream yet marking the boat to remember?"

entries.zh: 於是下詔擇京官有善政者補刺史，歲十月，按察使校殿最，自第一至第五，校考使及戶部長官總核之，以為升降。
entries.en: The throne then chose capital officials with good records for prefectures; each tenth month investigators graded them from first to fifth rank, and review commissioners with the revenue chief determined promotions.
entries.literal: An edict was then issued choosing capital officials with good administration to fill prefect posts; each year in the tenth month investigating commissioners graded excellence from first to fifth, and review commissioners with the head of the Ministry of Revenue totaled them for promotion and demotion.

entries.zh: 凡官，不曆州縣不擬台省。
entries.en: In general, officials who had not served locally were not nominated for central posts.
entries.literal: In general, officials who had not served in prefectures and counties were not nominated for central departments.

entries.zh: 已而悉集新除縣令宣政殿，親臨問以治人之策，而擢其高第者。
entries.en: He then assembled new magistrates in the Hall of Proclaiming Governance, questioned them on governance, and promoted the best answers.
entries.literal: Soon all newly appointed magistrates were gathered in the Hall of Proclaiming Governance; the emperor personally questioned them on policies for governing men and promoted those of highest grade.

entries.zh: 又詔員外郎、御史諸供奉官，皆進名敕授，而兵、吏部各以員外郎一人判南曹，由是銓司之任輕矣。
entries.en: Aides, censors, and palace attendants were ordered to submit names for direct appointment; each of the war and personnel ministries assigned one aide to the southern registry, lightening the evaluation offices' role.
entries.literal: An edict also ordered that aide officials, censors, and all palace attendants advance names for edict appointment; the Ministries of War and Personnel each had one aide judge the southern registry, and thus the evaluation offices' duties grew lighter.

entries.zh: 其後戶部侍郎宇文融又建議置十銓，乃以禮部尚書蘇頲等分主之。
entries.en: Later Yuwen Rong proposed ten evaluation boards, with Su Ting and others placed in charge.
entries.literal: Later Vice Minister of Revenue Yuwen Rong again proposed establishing ten evaluation boards, and Minister of Rites Su Ting and others were assigned to divide supervision.

entries.zh: 太子左庶子吳兢諫曰：「《易》稱'君子思不出其位'，言不侵官也。
entries.en: Wu Jing remonstrated: "The Changes says the noble man does not think beyond his post—one must not usurp another's duties.
entries.literal: Left Companion of the Heir Apparent Wu Jing remonstrated: "The Changes says 'the noble man does not think beyond his post'—meaning one should not invade another's office.

entries.zh: 今以頲等分掌吏部選，而天子親臨決之，尚書、侍郎皆不聞參，議者以為萬乘之君，下行選事。」
entries.en: Now Su Ting and others run personnel selection while the emperor decides in person, leaving minister and vice ministers out—critics said the Son of Heaven was doing clerks' work."
entries.literal: Now Ting and others divide control of Personnel selection while the Son of Heaven personally decides—minister and vice ministers all unheard from; critics held that the lord of ten thousand chariots was personally conducting selection below."

entries.zh: 帝悟，遂復以三銓還有司。
entries.en: The emperor took the point and restored the three boards to the regular ministries.
entries.literal: The emperor understood and returned the three evaluation boards to the regular offices.

entries.zh: 開元十八年，侍中裴光庭兼吏部尚書，始作循資格，而賢愚一概，必與格合，乃得銓授，限年躡級，不得逾越。
entries.en: In Kaiyuan 18, Pei Guangting as chief minister and personnel minister introduced seniority rules: worthy and unworthy alike had to match the schedule, advancing rank by rank without skipping years.
entries.literal: In the eighteenth year of Kaiyuan, Chief Minister Pei Guangting also served as Minister of Personnel and first made seniority regulations; worthy and foolish were treated alike—one had to match the regulation to receive evaluation appointment, years limited step by step, none could overstep.

entries.zh: 於是久淹不收者皆便之，謂之「聖書」。
entries.en: Long-stalled candidates welcomed it and called it the "sage's writ."
entries.literal: Thus those long detained without appointment all found it convenient and called it the "sage's writ."

entries.zh: 及光庭卒，中書令蕭嵩以為非求材之方，奏罷之。
entries.en: After Guangting died, Xiao Song argued it was not a way to find talent and had it abolished.
entries.literal: When Guangting died, Secretariat Director Xiao Song held it not the way to seek talent and memorialized to abolish it.

entries.zh: 乃下詔曰：「凡人年三十而出身，四十乃得從事，更造格以分寸為差，若循新格，則六十未離一尉。
entries.en: An edict said: "Men normally enter service at thirty and take active posts at forty; under the new minute grades, a man might still be a captain at sixty.
entries.literal: An edict was issued: "Ordinary men enter office at thirty and may begin active service at forty; remade regulations differ by minute grades—if one follows the new regulation, at sixty one has not yet left a captaincy.

entries.zh: 自今選人才業優異有操行及遠郡下寮名跡稍著者，吏部隨材甄擢之。」
entries.en: Henceforth the Ministry of Personnel should promote candidates of outstanding talent, conduct, or local reputation without waiting on the schedule."
entries.literal: From now in selection, those of outstanding talent and conduct, and lower aides in distant commanderies whose names and traces are somewhat notable—the Ministry of Personnel shall select and promote according to ability."

entries.zh: 凡選有文、武，文選吏部主之，武選兵部主之，皆為三銓，尚書、侍郎分主之。
entries.en: Selection was divided into civil and military tracks: the Ministry of Personnel oversaw civil appointments, the Ministry of War military ones. Each route used three evaluation boards, with ministers and vice-ministers taking charge in turn.
entries.literal: In general, selection had civil and military [branches]; civil selection was headed by the Ministry of Personnel, military selection by the Ministry of War; each was organized as three boards of evaluation, with ministers and vice-ministers dividing supervision among them.

entries.zh: 貞觀初，戶不及三百萬，絹一匹易米一斗。
entries.en: Early in Zhenguan there were fewer than three million households, and one bolt of silk bought only one dou of rice.
entries.literal: Early in Zhenguan, households numbered less than three million; one bolt of silk bought one dou of rice.

entries.zh: 至四年，米斗四五錢，外戶不閉者數月，馬牛被野，人行數千里不賫糧，民物蕃息，四夷降附者百二十萬人。
entries.en: By the fourth year rice cost four or five cash per dou; outer gates stood open for months; horses and cattle grazed freely; travelers went thousands of li without provisions; population and wealth grew; and 1.2 million frontier peoples submitted.
entries.literal: By the fourth year, rice was four or five cash per dou; outer gates went unbarred for months; horses and cattle roamed the wilds; travelers went thousands of li without carrying grain; people and goods flourished; a million two hundred thousand of the four barbarians submitted.

entries.zh: 是歲，天下斷獄，死罪者二十九人，號稱太平。
entries.en: That year only twenty-nine death sentences were handed down empire-wide—the age was called Great Peace.
entries.literal: That year, capital cases throughout the realm numbered twenty-nine death sentences; it was called the Great Peace.

entries.zh: 此高祖、太宗致治之大略，及其成效如此。
entries.en: Such was the broad policy by which Gaozu and Taizong brought order—and such were its results.
entries.literal: This was the great outline by which Gaozu and Taizong brought order, and such were its results.

entries.zh: 唐之始時，授人以口分、世業田，而取之以租、庸、調之法，其用之也有節。
entries.en: When the Tang was founded, the state allotted per-capita and hereditary fields and collected zu, yong, and diao levies—and spending stayed within bounds.
entries.literal: At the Tang's beginning, men were granted koufen and shiye fields, and taxes were taken by the zu, yong, and diao method; expenditures were also restrained.

entries.zh: 蓋其畜兵以府衛之制，故兵雖多而無所損；
entries.en: Soldiers were raised through the fubing militia and guard-garrison system, so a large army did not bankrupt the realm;
entries.literal: For they maintained troops by the fubing and guard-garrison system, so though troops were many there was no drain;

entries.zh: 設官有常員之數，故官不濫而易祿。
entries.en: each post had a fixed headcount, so offices were not overfilled and salaries remained payable.
entries.literal: offices were established with fixed quotas, so offices were not excessive and salaries were easy to pay.

entries.zh: 雖不及三代之盛時，然亦可以為經常之法也。
entries.en: It fell short of the golden ages of antiquity, yet it could still stand as a durable fiscal order.
entries.literal: Though it did not match the flourishing age of the Three Dynasties, it could still serve as regular law.

entries.zh: 及其弊也，兵冗官濫，為之大蠹。
entries.en: In time the system rotted: bloated armies and swollen bureaucracy became its gravest blight.
entries.literal: When it declined, redundant troops and excessive offices became a great plague.

entries.zh: 自天寶以來，大盜屢起，方鎮數叛，兵革之興，累世不息，而用度之數，不能節矣。
entries.en: After the Tianbao years, major rebellions broke out again and again, frontier governors turned traitor one after another, and war ran on for generations. The budget could no longer be held in check.
entries.literal: From the Tianbao era onward, great bandits arose repeatedly, regional commanders rebelled again and again, warfare flared generation after generation without cease, and the figures for expenditure could no longer be restrained.

entries.zh: 加以驕君昏主，奸吏邪臣，取濟一時，屢更其制，而經常之法，蕩然盡矣。
entries.en: Arrogant emperors and muddled courts, venal clerks and scheming ministers patched crises with stopgaps, rewrote the rules again and again, and the standing order vanished entirely.
entries.literal: Added to this were arrogant rulers and benighted sovereigns, corrupt officials and wicked ministers, seeking temporary relief and repeatedly changing the system until the regular laws were utterly swept away.

entries.zh: 由是財利之說興，聚斂之臣進。
entries.en: Profit-seeking theories spread, and men who lived to squeeze revenue rose to power.
entries.literal: Hence doctrines of profit arose and ministers of exaction advanced.

entries.zh: 蓋口分、世業之田壞而為兼並，租、庸、調之法壞而為兩稅。
entries.en: Per-capita and hereditary allotments collapsed into large estates; the zu-yong-diao levies gave way to the dual tax.
entries.literal: The koufen and shiye fields were destroyed and became consolidated holdings; the zu, yong, and diao system was destroyed and became the dual tax.

entries.zh: 至於鹽鐵、轉運、屯田、和糴、鑄錢、括苗、榷利、借商、進奉、獻助，無所不為矣。
entries.en: Salt and iron monopolies, transport offices, military farms, forced purchases of grain, minting, land surveys, excise levies, loans to merchants, court tribute, and "voluntary" gifts—every expedient was tried.
entries.literal: As for salt and iron monopolies, transport commissions, garrison farming, government grain purchases, coinage, land surveys, state monopolies, loans to merchants, tribute deliveries, and voluntary contributions—nothing was left undone.

entries.zh: 蓋愈煩而愈弊，以至於亡焉。
entries.en: The more tangled the system grew, the worse it failed—until the dynasty fell.
entries.literal: The more elaborate it grew, the more corrupt it became, until the dynasty perished.

entries.zh: 玄宗初立求治，蠲徭役者給蠲符，以流外及九品京官為蠲使，歲再遣之。
entries.en: When Xuanzong first sought reform, corvée exemptions were issued on tallies; minor officials and ninth-rank capital appointees served as exemption commissioners, sent out twice a year.
entries.literal: When Xuanzong first took the throne seeking good government, those exempted from corvée received exemption tallies; officials outside the regular roster and capital officials of the ninth rank served as exemption commissioners, dispatched twice yearly.

entries.zh: 開元八年，頒庸調法於天下，好不過精，惡不至濫，闊者一尺八寸，長者四丈。
entries.en: In Kaiyuan 8 the yong-diao standards were issued empire-wide: finest cloth not above refined grade, poorest not below acceptable; width at least 1.8 chi, length at most 4 zhang.
entries.literal: In the eighth year of Kaiyuan, the yong and diao law was promulgated empire-wide: the finest not beyond refined quality, the poorest not below acceptable grade; width at least one chi eight cun, length at most four zhang.

entries.zh: 然是時天下戶未嘗升降。
entries.en: Yet household registers had never been properly updated.
entries.literal: Yet at this time household registers throughout the realm had never been revised up or down.

entries.zh: 監察御史宇文融獻策：括籍外羨田、逃戶，自占者給復五年，每丁稅錢千五百，以攝御史分行括實。
entries.en: Censor Yuwen Rong proposed surveying hidden land and unregistered households: voluntary registration won five years' relief; each adult male paid 1,500 cash; acting censors fanned out to verify the rolls.
entries.literal: Supervising Censor Yuwen Rong proposed a plan: register surplus fields and absconding households outside the rolls; self-reporting received five years' exemption; each ding paid 1,500 cash in tax; acting censors were sent in branches to verify and register.

entries.zh: 陽翟尉皇甫憬上書言其不可。
entries.en: Yangdi Assistant Magistrate Huangfu Jing memorialized against the plan.
entries.literal: Assistant Magistrate of Yangdi Huangfu Jing memorialized that it should not be done.

entries.zh: 玄宗方任用融，乃貶憬為盈川尉。
entries.en: Xuanzong, backing Rong, demoted Jing to magistrate of Yingchuan.
entries.literal: Xuanzong was then employing Rong and demoted Jing to Assistant Magistrate of Yingchuan.

entries.zh: 諸道所括得客戶八十余萬，田亦稱是。
entries.en: The circuits registered over 800,000 client households, with land to match.
entries.literal: The various circuits registered more than eight hundred thousand client households, and fields in proportion.

entries.zh: 州縣希旨張虛數，以正田為羨，編戶為客，歲終，籍錢數百萬緡。
entries.en: Local officials eager to please inflated the rolls, reclassified regular land as surplus and registered households as clients, and by year-end reported several million strings in revenue.
entries.literal: Prefectures and counties, eager to please, inflated false figures, treating regular fields as surplus and registered households as clients; by year's end they registered several million strings in cash.

entries.zh: 明年，又詔民三歲以下為黃，十五以下為小，二十以下為中。
entries.en: The next year, children under three were infants, under fifteen minors, and under twenty youths.
entries.literal: The next year, an edict made those under three huang, under fifteen xiao, and under twenty zhong.

entries.zh: 又以民間戶高丁多者，率與父母別籍異居，以避征戍，乃詔十丁以上免二丁，五丁以上免一丁，侍丁孝者免徭役。
entries.en: Wealthy households with many sons often split registers to evade conscription; households of ten ding lost two, of five lost one, and filial attendants were exempt from corvée.
entries.literal: Because wealthy households with many adult males commonly split registers and lived apart from parents to avoid conscription, an edict exempted two ding from households of ten or more and one from five or more; filial attendants were exempt from corvée.

entries.zh: 天寶三載，更民十八以上為中男，二十三以上成丁。
entries.en: In Tianbao 3, males of eighteen became youths and those of twenty-three became adult males liable for tax.
entries.literal: In the third year of Tianbao, males eighteen and above became zhongnan; twenty-three and above became ding.

entries.zh: 五載，詔貧不能自濟者，每鄉免三十丁租庸。
entries.en: In Tianbao 5, each district exempted thirty ding from zu-yong for households too poor to survive.
entries.literal: In the fifth year, an edict exempted thirty ding per district from zu-yong for those too poor to support themselves.

entries.zh: 男子七十五以上、婦人七十以上，中男一人為侍；
entries.en: For men seventy-five and women seventy, one youth was assigned as attendant;
entries.literal: For men seventy-five and above and women seventy and above, one zhongnan served as attendant;

entries.zh: 八十以上以令式從事。
entries.en: those eighty and above were governed by special statute.
entries.literal: those eighty and above were treated according to statute.

entries.zh: 是時，海內富實，米鬥之價錢十三，青、齊間鬥才三錢，絹一匹錢二百。
entries.en: The empire was prosperous: rice cost thirteen cash per dou, only three in Qing and Qi, and two hundred cash per bolt of silk.
entries.literal: At this time the realm was rich and solid: rice thirteen cash per dou; in Qing and Qi only three cash; one bolt of silk two hundred cash.

entries.zh: 道路列肆，具酒食以待行人，店有驛驢，行千里不持尺兵。
entries.en: Roadside shops offered food and drink; inns kept relay donkeys; travelers went a thousand li unarmed.
entries.literal: Shops lined the roads with food and drink for travelers; inns had relay donkeys; one traveled a thousand li without carrying a weapon.

entries.zh: 天下歲入之物，租錢二百余萬緡，粟千九百八十余萬斛，庸、調絹七百四十萬匹，綿百八十余萬屯，布千三十五萬余端。
entries.en: Annual revenue: over two million strings in grain tax cash, nearly twenty million hu of grain, 7.4 million bolts of yong-diao silk, 1.8 million tun of cotton, and over ten million duan of cloth.
