entries.literal: Fangli's generals Lü Zhen and Ma Shuang fought at Jiaogang and were defeated by Kexiu; ten thousand heads were cut off, Zhen and others were captured, and Wu'an, Linming, Handan, and Shahe were taken.

entries.zh: 克用以安金俊為邢州刺史，招撫之。
entries.en: Keyong appointed An Jinjun governor of Xing Prefecture to pacify the region.
entries.literal: Keyong appointed An Jinjun governor of Xing Prefecture to win the people over.

entries.zh: 方立丐兵於王镕，镕以兵三萬赴之，克修還。
entries.en: Fangli begged Wang Rong for troops; Rong sent thirty thousand men, and Kexiu withdrew.
entries.literal: Fangli begged troops from Wang Rong; Rong sent thirty thousand men to his aid, and Kexiu withdrew.

entries.zh: 後二年，方立督部將奚忠信兵三萬攻遼州，以金啖赫連鐸與連和。
entries.en: Two years later Fangli led his subordinate Xi Zhongxin with thirty thousand men against Liao Prefecture and bribed Helian Duo with gold to join him.
entries.literal: Two years later Fangli supervised his subordinate Xi Zhongxin with thirty thousand troops to attack Liao Prefecture, bribing Helian Duo with gold to join in alliance.

entries.zh: 會契丹攻鐸，師失期，忠信三分其兵，鼓而行，克用伏兵於險，忠信前軍沒。
entries.en: The Khitans attacked Duo and the army missed its rendezvous. Zhongxin divided his force in three and advanced with drums beating. Keyong ambushed them in a defile and destroyed the vanguard.
entries.literal: It happened that the Khitans attacked Duo; the army missed its rendezvous. Zhongxin divided his force in three and advanced with drums beating. Keyong ambushed in a defile and Zhongxin's vanguard was wiped out.

entries.zh: 既戰，大敗，執忠信，餘眾走，脫歸者才十二。
entries.en: They were routed in battle; Zhongxin was captured, the rest fled, and only twelve men made it back alive.
entries.literal: After the battle they were greatly defeated; Zhongxin was captured, the rest fled, and only twelve men escaped back alive.

entries.zh: 龍紀元年，克用使李罕之、李存孝擊邢，攻磁、洺，方立戰琉璃陂，大敗，禽其二將，被斧锧，徇邢壘，呼曰：「孟公速降，有能斬其首者，假三州節度使！」
entries.en: In the first year of Longji, Keyong sent Li Hanzhi and Li Cunxiao against Xing and Ci-Ming. Fangli fought at Liuli Po and was routed; two generals were captured, shackled, and paraded before the Xing ramparts with the cry, "Lord Meng, surrender at once! Whoever cuts off his head shall govern the three prefectures!"
entries.literal: In the first year of Longji, Keyong sent Li Hanzhi and Li Cunxiao to attack Xing and assault Ci and Ming. Fangli fought at Liuli Po and was greatly defeated; his two generals were captured, put in cangue and stocks, and paraded before the Xing ramparts with the cry, "Lord Meng, surrender quickly! Whoever can cut off his head shall be made provisional military governor of the three prefectures!"

entries.zh: 方立力屈，又屬州殘墮，人心恐。
entries.en: Fangli's strength was spent, the prefectures lay in ruins, and panic spread through the ranks.
entries.literal: Fangli's strength was spent, and moreover the prefectures were ruined and collapsing; hearts were filled with fear.

entries.zh: 性剛急，持下少恩，夜自行陴，兵皆倨，告勞。
entries.en: Harsh and impatient by nature, he showed little kindness below. He patrolled the ramparts by night himself; the troops grew insolent and complained of exhaustion.
entries.literal: By nature he was harsh and impatient, showing little kindness to subordinates. He walked the ramparts by night himself; the troops were all insolent and complained of exhaustion.

entries.zh: 自顧不可復振，乃還，引冘殺。
entries.en: Seeing he could not recover, he returned and hanged himself.
entries.literal: Seeing that he could not rise again, he returned and took his own life by strangulation.

entries.zh: 二王諸葛李孟
entries.en: The Two Wangs, Zhu, Ge, Li, and Meng
entries.literal: The Two Wangs, Zhu, Ge, Li, and Meng

entries.zh: 黃巢入長安，所在盜興，陳人詣節度府，請犨為刺史，表於朝，授之。
entries.en: When Huang Chao entered Chang’an, brigands sprang up everywhere. The people of Chen went to the circuit seat and asked that Chou be made prefect; the court was petitioned, and the appointment was granted.
entries.literal: When Huang Chao entered Chang’an, bandits rose everywhere; the people of Chen went to the circuit headquarters requesting Chou as prefect, memorialized the court, and he was appointed.

entries.zh: 既視事，會官屬計曰：「巢若不死長安，必東出關，陳其沖也。」
entries.en: As soon as he took office he called his staff together and said, “If Huang Chao does not die in Chang’an, he will surely march east through the passes—and Chen stands in his path.”
entries.literal: Once he took office, he gathered officials and staff to plan, saying, “If Chao does not die in Chang’an, he must surely go east out through the pass—Chen is its choke point.”

entries.zh: 乃培城疏塹，實倉庫，峙槁薪，為守計。
entries.en: He raised the walls, cleared the moat, filled the granaries, stacked fuel, and prepared for a siege.
entries.literal: Thereupon he heightened the walls, dredged the moat, filled the granaries, piled firewood, and made plans for defense.

entries.zh: 民有貲者悉內之，繕甲兵，募悍勇，悉補子弟領兵。
entries.en: Wealthy citizens poured in their resources; he repaired arms and armor, recruited the toughest fighters, and placed his own kin in command of every unit.
entries.literal: Wealthy commoners all contributed inward; he repaired armor and weapons, recruited fierce and brave men, and all supplemented them with family sons and younger brothers to lead troops.

entries.zh: 巢敗，果東奔。
entries.en: When Huang Chao was defeated he did indeed flee eastward.
entries.literal: Chao was defeated and indeed fled east.

entries.zh: 賊將孟楷以萬人寇項，犨擊禽之。
entries.en: The rebel general Meng Kai invaded Xiang with ten thousand men, but Chou attacked and took him prisoner.
entries.literal: The bandit general Meng Kai with ten thousand men raided Xiang; Chou attacked and captured him.

entries.zh: 僖宗嘉其功，遷累檢校司空。
entries.en: Emperor Xizong praised his achievement and promoted him step by step to Acting Minister of Works.
entries.literal: Emperor Xizong praised his achievement and repeatedly promoted him to Acting Minister of Works.

entries.zh: 巢聞楷死，驚且怒，悉軍據溵水，與秦宗權合兵數十萬，繚長壕五周，百道攻之。
entries.en: Huang Chao, hearing that Kai was dead, was shocked and furious. He massed his entire army on the Yin River, joined Qin Zongquan for a force of hundreds of thousands, dug five rings of trenches around the city, and assaulted it from every side.
entries.literal: Chao heard that Kai was dead, was shocked and angry, mustered the entire army and held the Yin River, joined Qin Zongquan’s troops to several hundred thousand, encircled with long trenches five rounds deep, and attacked along a hundred routes.

entries.zh: 州人大恐，犨令曰：「士貴建功立名節，今雖眾寡不敵，男子當死地求生，徒懼無益也。
entries.en: The people of the prefecture were terrified. Chou proclaimed, “A true soldier wins fame by deeds of honor. Though we are outnumbered, a man should fight where death is certain if he hopes to live—fear alone will save no one.
entries.literal: The people of the prefecture were greatly afraid; Chou ordered, saying, “Gentlemen value establishing achievement and preserving integrity and reputation; though now few cannot match many, a man should seek life in a place of certain death—mere fear is of no use.

entries.zh: 且死國，不愈生為賊乎？
entries.en: Is it not better to die for one’s country than to live on as a rebel’s slave?
entries.literal: Moreover, to die for the state—is it not better than living as a bandit?

entries.zh: 吾家食陳祿，誓破賊以保陳，異議者斬！」
entries.en: My family has eaten Chen’s grain. I swear to break these rebels and save the city—and anyone who disagrees will be beheaded!”
entries.literal: My family eats Chen’s salary; I swear to break the bandits to preserve Chen—whoever disagrees will be beheaded!”

entries.zh: 眾聽命。
entries.en: The people obeyed.
entries.literal: The masses obeyed the command.

entries.zh: 引銳士出戰，屢破賊。
entries.en: He led his best troops out again and again and repeatedly routed the rebels.
entries.literal: He led crack troops out to battle and repeatedly defeated the bandits.

entries.zh: 巢益怒，將必屠之，乃起八仙營於州左，僭象宮闕，列百官曹署，儲糧為持久計。
entries.en: Huang Chao, growing still angrier, resolved to slaughter the city to the last man. He built an “Eight Immortals” camp east of the walls, mock palaces and halls, offices for a full bureaucracy, and stockpiled grain for a long siege.
entries.literal: Chao grew angrier and was determined to massacre them; thereupon he raised the Eight Immortals Camp east of the prefecture, presumptuously imitating palace gates and towers, arrayed the hundred officials’ bureaus, and stored grain for a prolonged plan.

entries.zh: 宗權輸鎧仗軍須，賊益張。
entries.en: Qin Zongquan sent armor, arms, and supplies, and the rebels grew bolder still.
entries.literal: Zongquan supplied armor, weapons, and military necessities; the bandits grew still more arrogant.

entries.zh: 犨小大數百戰，勝負相當，故人心固，乃間道乞師於朱全忠。
entries.en: Chou fought hundreds of engagements, great and small, with roughly even success, which kept morale firm. Meanwhile he sent secret envoys to Zhu Quanzhong begging for reinforcements.
entries.literal: Chou fought several hundred battles large and small; victories and defeats were roughly equal; therefore hearts were firm; then by a secret path he begged troops from Zhu Quanzhong.

entries.zh: 未幾，汴軍至，壁西北，陳人思奮，犨引兵急擊賊，破之。
entries.en: Before long the Bian army arrived and camped to the northwest. The people of Chen took heart, and Chou led a fierce assault that broke the rebel lines.
entries.literal: Before long the Bian troops arrived and encamped northwest; the people of Chen thought to exert themselves; Chou led troops in urgent attack on the bandits and broke them.

entries.zh: 圍凡三百日而解。
entries.en: The siege lasted three hundred days in all before it was lifted.
entries.literal: The siege in all lasted three hundred days before it was lifted.

entries.zh: 犨悉忠力以孤城抗賊，巢卒敗亡。
entries.en: Chou poured all his loyalty and strength into holding a single city against the rebels, and Huang Chao was ultimately destroyed.
entries.literal: Chou exhausted loyalty and strength to hold a lone city against the bandits; Chao ultimately was defeated and perished.

entries.zh: 然附全忠，亦賴其力復振，故委輸調發助全忠，常先它鎮雲。
entries.en: Yet he also leaned on Zhu Quanzhong and owed his recovery to Zhu’s power, so his supplies and levies went to aid Zhu first—ahead of every other circuit, men said.
entries.literal: Yet he attached himself to Quanzhong and also relied on his strength to revive; therefore tribute transport and dispatch assisted Quanzhong, often ahead of other circuits, it is said.

entries.zh: 昶帥忠武，珝遷行軍司馬。
entries.en: When Chang took command of the Zhongwu Army, Pin was made campaigning vice marshal.
entries.literal: Chang commanded the Zhongwu Army; Pin was transferred to campaigning Vice Marshal.

entries.zh: 昶之喪，知忠武留後，政簡濟，上下安之。
entries.en: After Chang’s death he served as acting governor of the Zhongwu Army. His rule was plain and effective, and officers and men alike were content.
entries.literal: At Chang’s mourning, he acted as Zhongwu military governor designate; his governance was simple and effective, and superiors and subordinates were at peace.

entries.zh: 全忠表為忠武軍節度使。
entries.en: Zhu Quanzhong petitioned the court to appoint him military governor of the Zhongwu Army.
entries.literal: Quanzhong memorialized the court to make him Zhongwu Army military governor.

entries.zh: 陳土惡善圮，珝疊甓表墉，遂無患。
entries.en: Chen’s poor soil made the walls prone to collapse; Pin faced them with layers of brick, and the problem ceased.
entries.literal: Chen’s soil was poor and prone to collapse; Pin stacked bricks facing the wall surface, and thereafter there was no trouble.

entries.zh: 三加檢校太保。
entries.en: He was three times promoted to Acting Grand Guardian.
entries.literal: Three times he was added Acting Grand Guardian.

entries.zh: 光化三年，同中書門下平章事，進兼侍中，封天水郡公。
entries.en: In the third year of Guanghua he was made Grand Councillor, promoted to concurrent Palace Attendant, and enfeoffed as Duke of Tianshui.
entries.literal: In the third year of Guanghua he became equal associate of the Secretariat-Chancellery, was advanced to concurrent Palace Attendant, and was enfeoffed as Duke of Tianshui commandery.

entries.zh: 按鄧艾故跡，決翟王渠溉稻以利農。
entries.en: Following the route of Deng Ai’s old canal, he opened the Zhaiwang Channel to irrigate the rice fields and benefit the farmers.
entries.literal: Following Deng Ai’s old traces, he opened the Zhaiwang Canal to irrigate rice fields for the benefit of agriculture.

entries.zh: 一家三節度，相繼二十餘年，陳人宜之。
entries.en: One family held three governorships in succession for more than twenty years, and the people of Chen were well content.
entries.literal: One family held three military governorships in succession for more than twenty years; the people of Chen found it fitting.

entries.zh: 先是，行密欲女镠子，镠急，乃遣元迎女，且告行密曰：「頵得誌，為患必大，請以子為質，願召還頵。」
entries.en: Earlier Xingmi had sought a marriage alliance with Liu’s son. In desperation Liu sent Yuan Guan to fetch the bride and told Xingmi, “If Yun succeeds the damage will be grave. Take my son as hostage and recall Yun.”
entries.literal: Earlier, Xingmi had wished to marry a daughter to Liu’s son; Liu was urgent and thereupon sent Yuan Guan to welcome the girl, and also told Xingmi, “If Yun succeeds, the harm will surely be great—please take my son as hostage and recall Yun.”

entries.zh: 行密使人謂頵曰：「不還，我遣人代守宣州。」
entries.en: Xingmi sent word to Yun: “If you do not return, I will send someone else to hold Xuanzhou.”
entries.literal: Xingmi sent someone to tell Yun, “If you do not return, I shall send someone to replace you in holding Xuanzhou.”

entries.zh: 頵不從。
entries.en: Yun refused.
entries.literal: Yun did not obey.

entries.zh: 镠輸錢二百萬緡犒軍，頵又請镠子元瓘出質，乃與綰引兵還。
entries.en: Liu paid two million strings of cash to reward the army. Yun also demanded that Liu’s son Yuan Guan be left as hostage. Only then did he withdraw with Xu Wan.
entries.literal: Liu supplied two million strings of cash to reward the army; Yun also asked that Liu’s son Yuan Guan come out as hostage; thereupon with Wan he led troops back.

entries.zh: 然內怨行密與镠，因移書曰：「侯王守方以奉天子，譬百川不朝於海，雖狂奔澶漫，終為涸土，不若順流無窮也。
entries.en: Yet he nursed resentment against Xingmi and Liu and wrote: “Princes hold their domains in service to the Son of Heaven. It is like the hundred streams not paying court to the sea—however wildly they rush and spread, they end as dry earth; better to follow the current without end.
entries.literal: Yet inwardly he resented Xingmi and Liu; therefore he sent a letter saying, “Marquises and kings guard their regions to serve the Son of Heaven—it is like the hundred streams not paying court to the sea; though they rush wildly and spread vast, in the end they become dry earth; it is not like following the current without end.

entries.zh: 東南揚為大，刀布金玉積如阜，願公上天子常賦，頵請悉儲峙，單車以從。」
entries.en: The southeast’s greatest power is Yangzhou, where gold and goods pile like hills. Go yourself to present the emperor’s regular tribute—I will store everything and follow you with a single cart.”
entries.literal: In the southeast Yang is greatest; knives, cloth, gold, and jade pile like mounds; I wish that you, sir, go up to the Son of Heaven with regular tribute—Yun asks to store and pile all of it and follow with a single cart.”

entries.zh: 行密答曰：「貢賦繇汴而達，適足資敵爾。」
entries.en: Xingmi answered, “Tribute must pass through Bianzhou—that would only arm our enemy.”
entries.literal: Xingmi replied, “Tribute and levies reach the court by way of Bian— that would only supply the enemy.”

entries.zh: 於是頵絕行密，大募兵。
entries.en: Yun then broke with Xingmi and raised a great army.
entries.literal: Thereupon Yun broke with Xingmi and recruited troops on a large scale.

entries.zh: 李神福白行密：「頵必叛，宜先圖之。」
entries.en: Li Shenfu warned Xingmi, “Yun will certainly rebel. You should strike first.”
entries.literal: Li Shenfu informed Xingmi, “Yun will surely rebel—you ought to plot against him first.”

entries.zh: 行密曰：「頵有大功，而反狀未明，殺之，諸將不為用。」
entries.en: Xingmi said, “Yun has rendered great service, and his treason is not yet proven. If I kill him, the other generals will not follow me.”
entries.literal: Xingmi said, “Yun has great achievements, and the signs of rebellion are not yet clear—if I kill him, the generals will not serve me.”

entries.zh: 頵遣其佐杜荀鶴至汴通好，全忠喜，屯宿州須變。
entries.en: Yun sent his aide Du Xunhe to Bian to treat with Zhu Quanzhong, who was delighted and encamped at Suzhou to await events.
entries.literal: Yun sent his aide Du Xunhe to Bian to open friendly relations; Quanzhong was pleased and encamped at Suzhou awaiting developments.

entries.zh: 行密以康儒在頵所，故授廬州刺史以間之。
entries.en: Because Kang Ru was with Yun, Xingmi appointed him prefect of Luzhou to drive a wedge between them.
entries.literal: Xingmi, because Kang Ru was at Yun’s place, therefore appointed him prefect of Luzhou to sow division.

entries.zh: 頵怒，族其家，儒曰：「公不用吾謀，死無地矣。」
entries.en: Yun, enraged, executed Kang Ru’s entire family. Ru said, “You would not heed my counsel—now I have nowhere to die but here.”
entries.literal: Yun was angry and exterminated his clan; Ru said, “My lord, you did not use my plan—I shall die with nowhere to be buried.”

entries.zh: 仁義焚東塘戰艦，夜攻常州，不克，轉戰至夾岡，立二幟，解甲而息，追兵莫敢向。
entries.en: Renyi burned his warships at Dongtang, attacked Changzhou by night without success, and fought his way to Jiagang. There he raised two banners, laid aside his armor, and rested—his pursuers dared not approach.
entries.literal: Renyi burned the warships at Dongtang, attacked Changzhou by night without taking it, fought on to Jiagang, set up two banners, removed armor and rested, and pursuing troops dared not advance.

entries.zh: 頵陳舟蕪湖。
entries.en: Yun stationed his fleet at Wuhu.
entries.literal: Yun arrayed boats at Wuhu.

entries.zh: 行密遣將王茂章攻潤州。
entries.en: Xingmi sent Wang Maozhang to attack Runzhou.
entries.literal: Xingmi sent the general Wang Maozhang to attack Runzhou.

entries.zh: 仁義以善射冠軍中，當時稱朱瑾槊，米誌誠弩，皆為第一。
entries.en: Renyi was the finest archer in the army. Men said Zhu Jin’s spear and Mi Zhicheng’s crossbow were each unmatched in their day.
entries.literal: Renyi for skill in archery topped the army; at the time they called Zhu Jin’s spear and Mi Zhicheng’s crossbow each first in their kind.

entries.zh: 仁義常曰：「誌誠弩十，不當瑾槊之一；
entries.en: Renyi used to say, “Ten of Mi Zhicheng’s bolts are not worth one thrust of Zhu Jin’s spear;
entries.literal: Renyi often said, “Ten of Zhicheng’s crossbow shots are not worth one of Jin’s spear thrusts;

entries.zh: 瑾槊十，不當吾弓之一。」
entries.en: and ten of Zhu Jin’s spear thrusts are not worth one shot from my bow.”
entries.literal: ten of Jin’s spear thrusts are not worth one of my bow shots.”

entries.zh: 人以為然。
entries.en: People believed him.
entries.literal: People thought it so.

entries.zh: 又其治軍嚴，善得士心。
entries.en: He also ran a strict camp and knew how to win his men’s loyalty.
entries.literal: Moreover, his governance of the army was strict, and he was good at winning soldiers’ hearts.

entries.zh: 戰卒數百，濠梁不毀，開門鬥，先告所當中，然後射之。
entries.en: With only a few hundred men at arms he left the moat bridge intact, opened the gate to fight, called out whom he would hit, and then shot—and hit.
entries.literal: With several hundred battle soldiers, the moat and bridge were not destroyed; he opened the gate to fight, first announcing whom he would hit, then shooting.

entries.zh: 茂章等不敢與確。
entries.en: Wang Maozhang and the others dared not close with him.
entries.literal: Maozhang and the others dared not engage him decisively.

entries.zh: 行密遣使謂曰：「吾不忘公功，能自歸，當復為行軍副使，但不可處兵。」
entries.en: Xingmi sent word: “I have not forgotten your service. Surrender and I will restore you as campaigning deputy—but you may not keep an army.”
entries.literal: Xingmi sent an envoy telling him, “I do not forget your achievements; if you can return of yourself, you shall again be campaigning deputy—but you may not hold troops.”

entries.zh: 仁義欲降，其子固諫，乃止。
entries.en: Renyi was ready to yield, but his son dissuaded him and he held back.
entries.literal: Renyi wished to surrender; his son firmly admonished him, and he stopped.

entries.zh: 頵善為治，資寬厚，通利商賈，民愛之。
entries.en: Yun was an able administrator—generous by nature, friendly to trade, and beloved by the people.
entries.literal: Yun was good at governance, by nature generous and mild, facilitated merchants’ profit, and the people loved him.

entries.zh: 善遇士，若楊夔、康軿、夏侯淑、殷文圭、王希羽等皆為上客。
entries.en: He treated scholars generously. Yang Kui, Kang Kai, Xiahou Shu, Yin Wengui, Wang Xiyu, and others were all honored as chief guests.
entries.literal: He treated scholars well; such men as Yang Kui, Kang Kai, Xiahou Shu, Yin Wengui, and Wang Xiyu were all honored guests.

entries.zh: 文圭有美名，全忠、镠交辟不應。
entries.en: Wengui enjoyed a fine reputation. Both Zhu Quanzhong and Qian Liu repeatedly invited him, but he refused them all.
entries.literal: Wengui had a fine reputation; Quanzhong and Liu repeatedly summoned him by turns, but he did not respond.

entries.zh: 頵置田宅，迎其母，以甥事之，故文圭為盡力。
entries.en: Yun gave him land and a house, welcomed his mother, and treated him as a sister’s son—so Wengui served him with all his strength.
entries.literal: Yun set up fields and a residence, welcomed his mother, and treated him as a sister’s son; therefore Wengui exerted himself to the utmost for him.

entries.zh: 夔知頵不足亢行密，著《溺賦》以戒，頵不用。
entries.en: Kui saw that Yun could not stand against Xingmi and wrote “The Rhapsody of Drowning” as a warning, but Yun ignored it.
entries.literal: Kui knew Yun was not sufficient to resist Xingmi; he composed “The Drowning Rhapsody” as a warning, but Yun did not use it.

entries.zh: 初，壽州刺史高彥溫舉州入朱全忠，行密襲之，諸將憚城堅不可拔，延壽鼓之，拔其城即表為淮南節度副使。
entries.en: Earlier, Gao Yanwen of Shouzhou had surrendered his prefecture to Zhu Quanzhong. When Xingmi attacked, the other generals feared the strong walls could not be taken. Yanshou rallied the men, took the city, and was at once made deputy military governor of Huainan.
entries.literal: Earlier, Shouzhou prefect Gao Yanwen had surrendered the entire prefecture to Zhu Quanzhong; Xingmi raided it; the generals feared the city’s stout walls could not be taken; Yanshou roused them, captured the city, and was immediately memorialized as Huainan military governor deputy.

entries.zh: 全忠猶屯壽春，延壽以新軍出，每旗五伍為列，遣李厚以十旗擊西偏，不勝，將斬之，厚請益五旗，殊死戰，全忠引去。
entries.en: Zhu Quanzhong still held Shouchun. Yanshou led out fresh troops in tight five-man squads under each banner and sent Li Hou with ten banners against the western flank. When Hou was beaten, Yanshou was about to execute him—but Hou begged for five more banners, fought desperately, and drove Zhu Quanzhong away.
entries.literal: Quanzhong was still encamped at Shouchun; Yanshou led out the new army, each banner in columns of five squads of five; he sent Li Hou with ten banners to strike the west flank; they did not win; he was about to behead Hou; Hou asked for five more banners, fought to the death, and Quanzhong withdrew.

entries.zh: 於是取黃、蘄、光三州，以功遷壽州團練使。
entries.en: He then seized Huang, Qi, and Guang prefectures and was made defense commissioner of Shouzhou for his merit.
entries.literal: Thereupon he took the three prefectures Huang, Qi, and Guang, and for his achievement was transferred to Shouzhou defense commissioner.

entries.zh: 昭宗在鳳翔，詔延壽圍蔡以披全忠勢，擢奉國軍節度使。
entries.en: While Emperor Zhaozong was at Fengxiang, Yanshou was ordered to besiege Cai and relieve Zhu Quanzhong’s pressure, and was promoted to military governor of the Fengguo Army.
entries.literal: When Emperor Zhaozong was at Fengxiang, an edict ordered Yanshou to besiege Cai to break Quanzhong’s momentum, and he was promoted to military governor of the Fengguo Army.

entries.zh: 全忠兵每至，延壽開門不設備，而不敢逼也。
entries.en: Whenever Zhu Quanzhong’s troops came up, Yanshou would open his gates without preparing defenses—yet they never dared press him.
entries.literal: Whenever Quanzhong’s troops arrived, Yanshou opened the gates without setting defenses, yet they dared not press him.

entries.zh: 延壽用軍常以寡鬥眾，敗還者盡斬之。
entries.en: Yanshou often fought larger forces with smaller ones, and beheaded every man who came back defeated.
entries.literal: Yanshou in using troops often fought many with few; those who returned defeated were all beheaded.

entries.zh: 田頵之附全忠，延壽陰約曰：「公有所為，我願執鞭。」
entries.en: When Tian Yun sided with Zhu Quanzhong, Yanshou secretly pledged, “Whatever you plan, sir, I am ready to serve at your side.”
entries.literal: When Tian Yun attached himself to Quanzhong, Yanshou secretly agreed, saying, “Whatever you undertake, sir, I wish to hold the whip.”

entries.zh: 頵喜，二人謀絕行密。
entries.en: Yun rejoiced, and the two plotted to destroy Yang Xingmi.
entries.literal: Yun was pleased; the two men plotted to cut off Xingmi.

entries.zh: 行密憂甚，紿病目，行觸柱僵。
entries.en: Xingmi was deeply worried. He pretended to be going blind, stumbled against a pillar, and collapsed.
entries.literal: Xingmi was deeply worried; he feigned eye disease, walked and struck a pillar and fell stiff.

entries.zh: 妻，延壽姊也，掖之。
entries.en: His wife—Yanshou’s elder sister—helped him up.
entries.literal: His wife was Yanshou’s elder sister; she supported him.

entries.zh: 行密泣曰：「吾喪明，諸子幼，得舅代我，無憂矣。」
entries.en: Xingmi wept and said, “I am going blind, and my sons are still young. With my uncle to take my place, I need fear nothing.”
entries.literal: Xingmi wept and said, “I have lost my sight; my sons are young—if I can have my uncle replace me, there will be no worry.”

entries.zh: 遣辯士召之，延壽疑，不肯赴。
entries.en: He sent an eloquent envoy to summon him, but Yanshou was suspicious and would not come.
entries.literal: He sent a persuasive speaker to summon him; Yanshou was suspicious and would not come.

entries.zh: 姊遣婢報故，延壽疾走揚州，拜未訖，士禽殺之，而廢其妻。
entries.en: His sister sent a maid with the truth. Yanshou raced to Yangzhou, but before he could finish his bow soldiers seized and killed him, and his wife was cast aside.
entries.literal: His sister sent a maid to report the truth; Yanshou raced to Yangzhou; before his bow was finished, soldiers seized and killed him, and his wife was deposed.

entries.zh: 贊曰：全忠，唐之盜也，行密誌梟其元而後已。
entries.en: The commentator says: Zhu Quanzhong was a robber of the Tang. Yang Xingmi swore he would not rest until Zhu’s head was spiked for all to see.
entries.literal: The commentator says: Quanzhong was a robber of Tang; Xingmi resolved to display his head on a pole before he would stop.

entries.zh: 田頵使出軍賦而助之，此其謀責難而絕之，非忠於唐也。
entries.en: When Tian Yun sent troops and supplies to aid Zhu, his aim was to hold Zhu accountable and then break with him—not loyalty to the Tang.
entries.literal: Tian Yun sent out army levies to aid him—this was his plan to press for accountability and cut him off; it was not loyalty to Tang.

entries.zh: 棄所附而覬尊大，亦已妄矣。
entries.en: To abandon his patron and reach for supremacy on his own was already folly.
entries.literal: To abandon whom he had attached himself to and covet supreme greatness was already delusion.

entries.zh: 孔子稱孟公綽為趙、魏老則優，不可以為滕、薛大夫。
entries.en: Confucius said Meng Gongchuo would excel as steward to the great houses of Zhao and Wei, but could not serve as minister to small states like Teng and Xue.
entries.literal: Confucius said that Meng Gongchuo as steward for Zhao and Wei would be excellent, but could not serve as grand officer of Teng and Xue.

entries.zh: 如仁厚、田、朱，材不足為吳、蜀之老，可與事天子哉！
entries.en: Men like Renhou, Tian, and Zhu lacked the talent even to be stewards in the kingdoms of Wu and Shu—how could they hope to serve the Son of Heaven!
entries.literal: Men like Renhou, Tian, and Zhu—their talent was insufficient to be stewards for Wu and Shu; how could they serve the Son of Heaven!

entries.zh: 行密使王茂章穴地取潤州，安仁義以家屬保城樓，兵不敢登。
entries.en: Xingmi had Wang Maozhang tunnel into Runzhou. Renyi put his family on the gate tower as a shield, and the attackers dared not climb up.
entries.literal: Xingmi had Wang Maozhang tunnel underground to take Runzhou; Renyi placed his family on the gate tower as protection, and troops dared not ascend.

entries.zh: 召李德誠曰：「汝可以委命。」
entries.en: He summoned Li Decheng and said, “You may trust me with your life.”
entries.literal: He summoned Li Decheng and said, “You may entrust your life to me.”

entries.zh: 乃抵弓矢就縛，父子斬揚州市。
entries.en: Then he laid down his bow, submitted to bonds, and he and his son were beheaded in Yangzhou.
entries.literal: Thereupon he set down bow and arrows and submitted to binding; father and son were beheaded in the Yangzhou marketplace.

entries.zh: 高趙田朱
entries.en: Biographies of Gao, Zhao, Tian, and Zhu.
entries.literal: Gao, Zhao, Tian, Zhu.

entries.zh: 又有崔承寵、楊偕、陳佑、崔清皆抗節忤賊，李文會指為沐黨，沐之死，皆被囚。
entries.en: Cui Chengbao, Yang Xie, Chen You, and Cui Qing also upheld their integrity and defied the rebels. Li Wenhu denounced them as Gao Mu's faction, and after Mu's death they were all imprisoned.
entries.literal: Also Cui Chengbao, Yang Xie, Chen You, and Cui Qing all upheld integrity and defied the rebels; Li Wenhu denounced them as Mu's faction; at Mu's death they were all imprisoned.

entries.zh: 劉悟既平師道，捉戶臂歔欷流涕，辟置義成節度府，亦請公度為僚屬。
entries.en: After Liu Wu had pacified Li Shidao, he took Guo Hu by the arm, weeping and sighing, and recruited him to the Yicheng military commissioner's staff. He also invited Li Gongdu as an aide.
entries.literal: After Liu Wu had pacified Shidao, he took Hu by the arm, weeping and sighing, and recruited him to the Yicheng military commissioner's staff; he also invited Gongdu as aide.

entries.zh: 元和十四年，贈沐吏部尚書，委馬揔備禮收葬，恤其家。
entries.en: In the fourteenth year of Yuanhe, Gao Mu was posthumously granted minister of personnel. Ma Cong was entrusted to prepare rites for his reburial and provide relief to his family.
entries.literal: In the fourteenth year of Yuanhe, Mu was posthumously granted Minister of Personnel; Ma Cong was entrusted to prepare rites for reburial and comfort his family.

entries.zh: 後署師道府屬。
entries.en: Later he was appointed to Li Shidao's staff.
entries.literal: Later he was appointed a staff member in Shidao's prefectural office.

entries.zh: 及師道不軌，提刀負棺入諫曰：「願前死，不見城之破。」
entries.en: When Li Shidao rebelled, he entered bearing a knife and a coffin on his back and admonished him: "Let me die first—I refuse to live to see this city taken."
entries.literal: When Shidao went astray from the right path, he took up a knife and shouldered a coffin, entering to remonstrate, saying, "I wish to die first—I cannot bear to see the city fall.

entries.zh: 又畫縛載檻車狀而妻子系累者以獻，師道怒，囚之。
entries.en: He also painted a picture of himself bound and loaded into a prison cart, with wife and children shackled together, and presented it. Li Shidao flew into a rage and had him imprisoned.
entries.literal: He also painted a scene of binding and loading into a caged cart, with wife and children tied together, and presented it. Shidao grew angry and imprisoned him.

entries.zh: 劉悟既入，釋其禁，辟署義成府。
entries.en: Once Liu Wu took control, he freed him and appointed him to the Yicheng military commissioner's staff.
entries.literal: After Liu Wu had entered, he released him from confinement and recruited him to the Yicheng prefectural staff.

entries.zh: 後徙潞，亦隨府遷。
entries.en: When the headquarters later moved to Lu Prefecture, he moved with them.
entries.literal: Later, when the office moved to Lu, he also followed the staff in its transfer.

entries.zh: 監軍劉承偕與悟不平，陰與慈州刺史張汶謀縛悟送闕下，以汶代節度。
entries.en: The army supervisor Liu Chengjie bore a grudge against Liu Wu and secretly plotted with Cizhou Prefect Zhang Wen to seize Liu Wu and send him to the capital, so that Zhang Wen could take his place as military commissioner.
entries.literal: Army supervisor Liu Chengjie was at odds with Wu; secretly he joined Cizhou prefect Zhang Wen in a plot to bind Wu and send him to the capital, with Wen replacing him as military commissioner.

entries.zh: 事泄，悟以兵圍承偕，殺小使，赴言遽入責曰：「司空縱兵脅天子使者，是欲效李司空邪？
entries.en: When the plot was exposed, Liu Wu surrounded Liu Chengjie with troops and killed his attendants. Jia Zhijan rushed in and upbraided him: "Commissioner, you have turned soldiers on the emperor's envoy—are you trying to follow in Li Shidao's footsteps?
entries.literal: The affair leaked out. Wu surrounded Chengjie with troops and killed his attendants. Zhijan hurried in and rebuked him, saying, "Sikong, you have loosed troops to coerce the Son of Heaven's envoy—do you mean to imitate Sikong Li?

entries.zh: 它日復為軍中所指笑。」
entries.en: One day the whole army will point at you and laugh."
entries.literal: Another day you will again be pointed at and laughed at in the army.

entries.zh: 悟聞，感悔，匿承偕於第以免。
entries.en: Liu Wu was moved to remorse and hid Liu Chengjie in his own mansion to protect him.
entries.literal: Wu heard this, was moved to repentance, and hid Chengjie in his residence to keep him from harm.

entries.zh: 悟每有過，必爭，故悟能以臣節光明於朝。
entries.en: Whenever Liu Wu erred, Jia Zhijan challenged him without fail, and so Liu Wu was able to uphold his loyalty before the throne.
entries.literal: Whenever Wu had a fault, Zhijan was sure to dispute it; therefore Wu was able to make his ministerial integrity shine at court.

entries.zh: 穆宗召為諫議大夫，群情灑然稱允。
entries.en: Emperor Muzong summoned him to serve as Remonstrance Grand Master, and the court received the appointment with universal approval.
entries.literal: Emperor Muzong summoned him as Remonstrance Grand Master; public sentiment was refreshed and all approved.

entries.zh: 而悟固留，得聽。
entries.en: Liu Wu insisted on keeping him, however, and the court allowed the appointment to wait.
entries.literal: But Wu firmly detained him, and the summons was granted a deferral.

entries.zh: 始，悟子從諫貴甚，見直言輒衣紫擁笏，以兵自衛。
entries.en: At first Liu Wu's son Liu Congjian carried himself with great arrogance; whenever he saw Jia Zhijan he would appear in purple robes with his court tablet in hand, surrounded by armed guards.
entries.literal: At first Wu's son Congjian was extremely haughty; whenever he saw Zhijan he would wear purple robes and clutch his court tablet, with soldiers guarding him.

entries.zh: 直言諫悟曰：「郎少年，毋使襲山東熊，朝服可擅著邪？」
entries.en: Jia Zhijan admonished Liu Wu: "Your son is still young—do not let him imitate the swaggering warlords of the east. Does he think court robes are his to put on whenever he pleases?"
entries.literal: Zhijan remonstrated with Wu, saying, "The young master is still a youth—do not let him take after the brutes of Shandong. May court dress be worn at will?

entries.zh: 悟死，從諫不發喪，召大將劉武德等矯悟遺言，與鄰道使共表求襲位，直言入讓曰：「父死不哭，何顏面見山東義士乎？」
entries.en: When Liu Wu died, Liu Congjian withheld the news of his death. He summoned the senior general Liu Wude and others to forge his father's dying instructions, then joined with envoys from neighboring circuits in a memorial asking to inherit the post. Jia Zhijan came in and rebuked him: "Your father is dead and you will not mourn—how will you ever face the loyal men of the east?"
entries.literal: When Wu died, Congjian did not announce the mourning. He summoned the great general Liu Wude and others to forge Wu's last words, and together with envoys from neighboring circuits submitted a memorial requesting succession. Zhijan entered and reproached him, saying, "Your father is dead and you do not weep—what face have you to show the righteous men of Shandong?"

entries.zh: 從諫曰：「欲反耳。」
entries.en: Liu Congjian replied, "I intend to rebel—that is all."
entries.literal: Congjian said, "I mean to rebel, that is all."

entries.zh: 直言仰天哭曰：「爾父提十二州地歸朝廷為功臣。
entries.en: Jia Zhijan lifted his face to heaven and wailed: "Your father surrendered twelve prefectures to the throne and died a honored servant of the empire.
entries.literal: Zhijan looked up to heaven and wept, saying, "Your father brought twelve prefectures back to the court and became a meritorious minister.

entries.zh: 然以張汶故，自謂不潔淋頭，卒羞死。
entries.en: Yet because of Zhang Wen he felt himself disgraced beyond cleansing and died in humiliation.
entries.literal: Yet because of Zhang Wen he considered himself defiled as if urine had been poured on his head, and in the end died of shame.

entries.zh: 郎今日乃欲反邪？」
entries.en: And now you mean to rebel?"
entries.literal: And today you, young master, wish to rebel?"

entries.zh: 從諫起抱直言項哭曰：「計窮而然。」
entries.en: Liu Congjian rose, threw his arms around Jia Zhijan's neck, and wept: "I am driven to this because I have no other way out."
entries.literal: Congjian rose, embraced Zhijan by the neck, and wept, saying, "Plans exhausted—that is why it has come to this."

entries.zh: 直言曰：「君何憂無土地，今脅朝廷，正速死耳。
entries.en: Jia Zhijan said, "Why worry about lacking territory? If you threaten the throne now, you will only bring on your own swift ruin.
entries.literal: Zhijan said, "My lord, why worry that you lack land? Now you coerce the court—you are merely hastening your death.

entries.zh: 若從武德謀，吾見劉氏為元濟矣。」
entries.en: If you follow Liu Wude's counsel, I see the Liu clan ending as Wu Yuanji did."
entries.literal: If you follow Wude's plot, I see the Liu house becoming Yuanji."

entries.zh: 從諫拜曰：「唯大夫救之。」
entries.en: Liu Congjian bowed low and said, "Only you can save me, sir."
entries.literal: Congjian bowed and said, "Only the Grand Master can save me."

entries.zh: 直言乃自攝留後，使從諫居喪。
entries.en: Jia Zhijan then assumed the acting post of military commissioner himself and put Liu Congjian into proper mourning.
entries.literal: Zhijan thereupon took the acting post of leave-behind commissioner himself and had Congjian observe mourning.

entries.zh: 初，從諫惟鄆兵二千同謀。
entries.en: At first only two thousand Yan troops were in on Liu Congjian's plot.
entries.literal: At first Congjian had only two thousand Yan troops as co-conspirators.

entries.zh: 直言既折之，軍中遂安。
entries.en: Once Jia Zhijan had broken their resolve, the army settled down.
entries.literal: Once Zhijan had broken their resolve, the army was thereafter settled.

entries.zh: ◎忠義下程千里，京兆萬年人。
entries.en: ◎ Loyalty and Righteousness (continued). Cheng Qianli was a native of Wannian in the Capital district.
entries.literal: ◎ Loyalty and Righteousness, Lower Section. Cheng Qianli was a native of Wannian in Jingzhao.

entries.zh: 長七尺，魁岸有力。
entries.en: He was seven feet tall, broad-shouldered and powerfully built.
entries.literal: He stood seven chi tall, with a towering frame and great strength.

entries.zh: 應募磧西，累官安西副都護。
entries.en: He enlisted in the western frontier armies and eventually became Vice Protector-General of Anxi.
entries.literal: He volunteered for service west of the Gobi and rose through successive posts to Vice Protector-General of Anxi.

entries.zh: 天寶末，兼北庭都護、安西北庭節度使。
entries.en: Late in the Tianbao reign, he also served as Protector-General of Beiting and as military commissioner over Anxi and Beiting.
entries.literal: At the end of the Tianbao era, he additionally held the posts of Protector-General of Beiting and Military Commissioner of Anxi and Beiting.

entries.zh: 突厥首領阿布思內附，本隸朔方，賜氏李，名獻忠，度屬幽州，素與安祿山有怨，內懼，故叛還磧外，數盜邊。
entries.en: The Turkic leader Abu Si had come over to the Tang and was originally assigned to Shuofang. The court gave him the surname Li and the name Xianzhong and placed him under Youzhou. He had long been at odds with An Lushan and, fearing for his safety, broke away to the outer steppe and repeatedly raided the frontier.
entries.literal: The Turkic chieftain Abu Si had submitted to the court and originally belonged to Shuofang; he was granted the surname Li and the name Xianzhong, was reassigned to Youzhou jurisdiction, had long harbored resentment against An Lushan, feared him inwardly, and therefore rebelled and returned beyond the desert frontiers, repeatedly raiding the border.

entries.zh: 玄宗患之，詔千里將兵討捕。
entries.en: The Xuanzong Emperor, alarmed by these raids, ordered Cheng Qianli to take troops in pursuit.
entries.literal: Emperor Xuanzong was troubled by this and ordered Cheng Qianli to lead troops to pursue and capture him.

entries.zh: 千里諭葛邏祿，陰令掎角。
entries.en: Cheng Qianli persuaded the Geluolu to join the campaign and quietly arranged a pincer attack.
entries.literal: Cheng Qianli instructed the Geluolu tribe and secretly directed them to attack from a second angle.

entries.zh: 獻忠果以窮歸葛邏祿，縛之，並妻子帳下數千人送千里所，乃獻俘勤政樓，詔斬以徇。
entries.en: Hemmed in, Xianzhong fled to the Geluolu, who seized him and, along with his family and several thousand of his followers, delivered the whole party to Cheng Qianli. He then presented the captive at Qinzheng Tower, where an imperial order had him executed as an example.
entries.literal: Xianzhong, driven to extremity, indeed submitted to the Geluolu, who bound him and, together with his wife, children, and several thousand followers in his camp, sent them to Cheng Qianli's headquarters. Thereupon he presented the captive at Qinzheng Tower; an edict ordered him beheaded as a public warning.

entries.zh: 擢千里右金吾衛大將軍，留宿衛。
entries.en: Cheng Qianli was promoted to grand general of the Right Gold Crow Guard and retained at court for palace duty.
entries.literal: Cheng Qianli was promoted to Grand General of the Right Gold Crow Guard and kept on palace night duty.

entries.zh: 所得奉祿，悉衣食人之孤遺者。
entries.en: Every penny of his salary went to clothe and feed orphans and the destitute.
entries.literal: Whatever salary he received he used entirely to clothe and feed orphans and the bereft.

entries.zh: 歲滿，笥余一縑，駕柴車去。
entries.en: When his term ended, only one bolt of silk remained in his box; he left in a firewood cart.
entries.literal: When his term ended, only one piece of silk remained in his chest; he drove off in a firewood cart.

entries.zh: 愛陸渾佳山水，乃定居。
entries.en: He loved the fine landscape of Luhun and made his home there.
entries.literal: He loved the fine mountains and waters of Luhun and settled there permanently.

entries.zh: 不為墻垣扃鑰，家無仆妾。
entries.en: He put up no walls or locks, and kept neither servants nor concubines.
entries.literal: He built no walls or bolts; his household had no servants or concubines.

entries.zh: 歲饑，日或不爨。
entries.en: In famine years he sometimes went whole days without lighting a fire.
entries.literal: In years of famine he sometimes went a day without cooking.

entries.zh: 嗜酒，陶然彈琴以自娛。
entries.en: He loved wine and would play the zither in tranquil delight to amuse himself.
entries.literal: He loved wine and would play the zither in serene pleasure to amuse himself.

entries.zh: 人以酒肴從之，不問賢鄙為酣飫。
entries.en: Whoever brought him food and drink, worthy or base, he would feast with them until all were satisfied.
entries.literal: When people brought him food and drink, he made no distinction between the worthy and the base, but feasted with all until satisfied.

entries.zh: 是時程休、邢宇、宇弟宙、張茂之、李、族子丹叔、惟嶽、喬潭、楊拯、房垂、柳識皆號門弟子。
entries.en: At that time Cheng Xiu, Xing Yu, Yu's younger brother Zhou, Zhang Mao-zhi, Li Shi, his clansmen Dan-shu and Wei-yue, Qiao Tan, Yang Zheng, Fang Chui, and Liu Shi were all known as his disciples.
entries.literal: At this time Cheng Xiu, Xing Yu, Yu's younger brother Zhou, Zhang Mao-zhi, Li, his clansmen Dan-shu and Wei-yue, Qiao Tan, Yang Zheng, Fang Chui, and Liu Shi were all called his disciples at the gate.

entries.zh: 德秀善文辭，作《蹇士賦》以自況。
entries.en: Dexiu excelled at letters and wrote "The Lame Gentleman Fu" to portray himself.
entries.literal: Dexiu was skilled in literary expression and wrote "The Lame Gentleman Fu" to portray his own situation.

entries.zh: 房琯每見德秀，嘆息曰：「見紫芝眉宇，使人名利之心都盡。」
entries.en: Whenever Fang Guan met Dexiu he would sigh and say: "A glimpse of Zizhi's countenance makes every craving for fame and gain disappear."
entries.literal: Whenever Fang Guan saw Dexiu, he would sigh: "To behold Zizhi's brow alone makes every thought of fame and profit vanish."

entries.zh: 蘇源明常語人曰：「吾不幸生衰俗，所不恥者，識元紫芝也。」
entries.en: Su Yuanming often told others: "Unhappy am I to have been born in a decadent age; the one thing I am not ashamed of is having known Yuan Zizhi."
entries.literal: Su Yuanming often said to others: "Unhappy am I to have been born in a declining age—the one thing I am not ashamed of is having known Yuan Zizhi."

entries.zh: 李華兄事德秀，而友蕭穎士、劉迅。
entries.en: Li Hua honored Dexiu as an elder brother and befriended Xiao Yingshi and Liu Xun.
entries.literal: Li Hua treated Dexiu as an elder brother, and was friends with Xiao Yingshi and Liu Xun.

entries.zh: 及卒，華謚曰文行先生。
entries.en: When he died, Hua gave him the posthumous title Master of Literary Conduct.
entries.literal: When Dexiu died, Hua gave him the posthumous title Master of Literary Conduct.

entries.zh: 天下高其行，不名，謂之元魯山。
entries.en: The empire revered his conduct and would not speak his personal name, calling him Yuan of Mount Lu instead.
entries.literal: The empire revered his conduct and would not speak his personal name, calling him instead Yuan of Mount Lu.

entries.zh: 華於是作《三賢論》。
entries.en: Hua thereupon wrote "An Essay on Three Worthies."
entries.literal: Hua thereupon wrote "An Essay on Three Worthies."

entries.zh: 或問所長，華曰：「德秀誌當以道紀天下，迅當以《六經》諧人心，穎士當以中古易今世。
entries.en: When asked what each excelled at, Hua said: "Dexiu aimed to order the empire by the Way; Xun aimed to harmonize men's hearts with the Six Classics; Yingshi aimed to replace the present age with the middle antiquity.
entries.literal: When asked wherein each excelled, Hua said: "Dexiu's intent was to order the empire by the Way; Xun's was to harmonize men's hearts with the Six Classics; Yingshi's was to replace the present age with the middle antiquity.

entries.zh: 德秀欲齊愚智，迅感一物不得其正，穎士呼吸折節而獲重祿，不易一刻之安易，於孔子之門，皆達者歟！
entries.en: Dexiu wished to level the foolish and the wise; Xun was stirred whenever a single thing fell short of its proper place; Yingshi would bend and bow with every breath to win heavy rewards, unwilling to trade a moment's ease—yet are all of these adept men within Confucius's gate?
entries.literal: Dexiu wished to make the foolish and the wise equal; Xun was moved whenever a single thing failed to attain its proper place; Yingshi would bend and bow for breath to obtain heavy emoluments, unwilling to trade one moment's ease—yet within Confucius's gate, are these all adept men?

entries.zh: 使德秀據師保之位，瞻形容，乃見其仁。
entries.en: Place Dexiu in the post of tutor and protector and look upon his face—then you see his humanity.
entries.literal: Let Dexiu occupy the position of tutor and protector, and gaze on his countenance—then you see his humanity.

entries.zh: 迅被卿佐服，居賓友，謀治亂根源，參乎元精，乃見其妙。
entries.en: Let Xun wear the robes of a chief minister's aide, dwell among guests and friends, and deliberate the roots of order and chaos while communing with the primordial essence—then you see his subtlety.
entries.literal: Let Xun wear the garb of a chief minister's aide and dwell among guests and friends, deliberating the roots of order and chaos and communing with the primordial essence—then you see his subtlety.

entries.zh: 穎士若百煉之剛，不可屈，使當廢興去就、一生一死間，而後見其節。
entries.en: Let Yingshi be steel tempered a hundred times, impossible to bend; set him at the turning point between a dynasty's rise and fall, between life and death—then you see his integrity.
entries.literal: Let Yingshi be steel refined a hundred times, impossible to bend; let him face the going and staying of dynasties, the single span between life and death—then you see his integrity.

entries.zh: 德秀以為王者作樂崇德，天人之極致，而辭章不稱，是無樂也，於是作《破陣樂辭》以訂商、周。
entries.en: Dexiu held that when kings made music to exalt virtue, that was the utmost of Heaven and man, yet unworthy words made it as though there were no music at all; he therefore composed lyrics for "Breaking the Battle Array" to correct the music of Shang and Zhou.
entries.literal: Dexiu held that when kings made music to exalt virtue, that was the utmost of Heaven and man, yet unworthy wording made it as if there were no music; he therefore composed lyrics for "Breaking the Battle Array" to correct the Shang and Zhou.

entries.zh: 迅世史官，述《禮》、《易》、《書》、《春秋》、《詩》為《古五說》，條貫源流，備古今之變。
entries.en: Xun, a historian of his age, set forth the Ritual, Changes, Documents, Annals, and Odes in "The Ancient Five Expositions," threading origins and developments and encompassing change from antiquity to the present.
entries.literal: Xun, being a historian of the age, set forth the Ritual, Changes, Documents, Annals, and Odes in "The Ancient Five Expositions," threading origins and developments and encompassing change ancient and modern.

entries.zh: 穎士尤罪子長不編年而為列傳，後世因之，非典訓也。
entries.en: Yingshi especially faulted Master Zichang for not compiling year-by-year annals and writing biographical accounts instead, which later generations followed—this was not canonical teaching.
entries.literal: Yingshi especially faulted Master Zi-chang for not compiling annals but writing biographical accounts, which later generations followed—this was not canonical instruction.

entries.zh: 自《春秋》三家後，非訓齊生人不錄。
entries.en: After the three schools of the Spring and Autumn, he recorded only what could instruct and regulate the living.
entries.literal: After the three schools of the Spring and Autumn, only what instructed and regulated the living was recorded.

entries.zh: 然各有病，元病酒，劉病賞物，蕭病貶惡太亟、獎能太重。
entries.en: Yet each had a flaw: Yuan's was wine; Liu's was cherishing possessions; Xiao's was condemning evil too harshly and praising talent too lavishly.
entries.literal: Yet each had a flaw: Yuan's flaw was wine; Liu's was cherishing possessions; Xiao's was condemning evil too urgently and praising talent too heavily.

entries.zh: 若取其節，皆可為人師也。」
entries.en: If you take their integrity alone, each could serve as another's teacher."
entries.literal: If you take their integrity, each could serve others as a teacher."

entries.zh: 世謂篤論。
entries.en: His contemporaries called this a sincere and weighty judgment.
entries.literal: The age called this sincere judgment.

entries.zh: 休，字士美，廣平人。
entries.en: Cheng Xiu, styled Shimei, was from Guangping.
entries.literal: Xiu, styled Shimei, was a man of Guangping.

entries.zh: 宇字紹宗，宙字次宗，河間人。
entries.en: Xing Yu, styled Shaozong, and his younger brother Zhou, styled Cizong, were from Hejian.
entries.literal: Yu, styled Shaozong; Zhou, styled Cizong—men of Hejian.

entries.zh: 茂之，字季豐，南陽人。
entries.en: Zhang Mao-zhi, styled Jifeng, was from Nanyang.
entries.literal: Mao-zhi, styled Jifeng, was a man of Nanyang.

entries.zh: 字伯高，丹叔字南誠，惟嶽字謨道，趙人。
entries.en: Li Shi, styled Bogao; his clansmen Dan-shu, styled Nancheng, and Wei-yue, styled Modao, were from Zhao.
entries.literal: [Li], styled Bogao; Dan-shu styled Nancheng; Wei-yue styled Modao—men of Zhao.

entries.zh: 潭字源，梁人。
entries.en: Qiao Tan, styled Yuan, was from Liang.
entries.literal: Tan, styled Yuan, was a man of Liang.

entries.zh: 垂，字翼明，清河人。
entries.en: Fang Chui, styled Yiming, was from Qinghe.
entries.literal: Chui, styled Yiming, was a man of Qinghe.

entries.zh: 拯，字齊物，隋觀王雄後，舉進士，終右驍衛騎曹參軍。
entries.en: Yang Zheng, styled Qiwu, a descendant of Sui's Prince of Guan Xiong, passed the jinshi examination and ended his career as cavalry retainer of the Right Martial Guards.
entries.literal: Zheng, styled Qiwu, a descendant of Sui's Prince of Guan Xiong, passed the jinshi examination, and ended as Cavalry Retainer of the Right Martial Guards.

entries.zh: 擢制科，遷南華令。
entries.en: Liu Shi passed the special examination and was appointed magistrate of Nanhua.
entries.literal: Selected in the special examination, he was transferred to be magistrate of Nanhua.

entries.zh: 大水，他縣饑，人至相屬，為具{衍食}鬻，及去，糗糧送之，吏為立碑。
entries.en: When great floods struck and neighboring counties starved, refugees came in an unbroken stream; he prepared thin gruel for them to buy, and when they departed he sent them off with dry provisions; the clerks erected a stele in his honor.
entries.literal: Great flood; other counties were stricken with famine and people came in succession; he provided thin gruel for sale, and when they left he sent them with dry provisions; the clerks erected a stele for him.

entries.zh: 安祿山亂，客清河，為乞師平原太守顏真卿，一郡獲全。
entries.en: During An Lushan's rebellion he stayed in Qinghe and begged Yan Zhenqing, prefect of Pingyuan, for troops, thereby preserving an entire commandery.
entries.literal: During An Lushan's rebellion he sojourned in Qinghe, pleaded for troops from Yan Zhenqing, prefect of Pingyuan, and one whole commandery was preserved.

entries.zh: 歷廬州刺史。
entries.en: He later served as prefect of Luzhou.
entries.literal: He served successively as prefect of Luzhou.

entries.zh: 拯與名最著，潭、識以文傳後。
entries.en: Zheng and Chui were most renowned; Tan and Shi handed their fame down through literature.
entries.literal: Zheng and E were most renowned; Tan and Shi passed their fame down through literature.

entries.zh: 自中原亂，士人率度江，李華、柳識、韓洄、王定皆仰臯節，與友善。
entries.en: After the central plains fell into chaos, scholar-officials mostly fled south across the Yangzi; Li Hua, Liu Shi, Han Hui, and Wang Ding all revered Gao's integrity and became his friends.
entries.literal: Since the central plains fell into chaos, scholar-officials mostly crossed the Yangzi; Li Hua, Liu Shi, Han Hui, and Wang Ding all looked up to Gao's integrity and befriended him.

entries.zh: 洄、定常評臯可為宰輔、師保；
entries.en: Hui and Ding often said that Gao was fit to serve as chief minister and royal tutor.
entries.literal: Hui and Ding often judged that Gao could serve as chief minister and tutor-protector.

entries.zh: 華亦以為分天下善惡，一人而已。
entries.en: Hua also held that to divide the empire's good and evil required only this one man.
entries.literal: Hua also held that to divide the empire's good and evil required only this one man.

entries.zh: 卒，年四十六，洄等制服行哭，詔贈秘書少監。
entries.en: He died at forty-six; Hui and the others wore mourning and followed the funeral procession weeping; an edict posthumously appointed him vice director of the Palace Library.
entries.literal: He died at forty-six; Hui and the others wore mourning and went weeping; an edict posthumously appointed him Vice Director of the Palace Library.

entries.zh: 元和中，謚為貞孝。
entries.en: In the Yuanhe era he was given the posthumous title Upright and Filial.
entries.literal: In the Yuanhe era he was given the posthumous title Upright and Filial.

entries.zh: 子德輿，至宰相，別傳。
entries.en: His son Deyu rose to grand councilor and is treated in a separate biography.
entries.literal: His son De-yu rose to Grand Councilor and has a separate biography.

entries.zh: 陽城，字亢宗，定州北平人，徙陜州夏縣，世為官族。
entries.en: Yang Cheng, styled Kangzong, was from Beiping in Dingzhou and later moved to Xia County in Shanzhou; his family had served as officials for generations.
entries.literal: Yang Cheng, styled Kangzong, was a native of Beiping in Dingzhou, moved to Xia County in Shanzhou, and for generations was an official clan.

entries.zh: 資好學，貧不能得書，求為吏，隸集賢院，竊院書讀之，晝夜不出戶，六年，無所不通。
entries.en: Though he loved learning, poverty kept him from books; he sought work as a clerk at the Hall of Assembled Worthies, stole books from the hall to read, and for six years never left his door until he had mastered everything.
entries.literal: Though he loved learning, he was too poor to obtain books; he sought to become a clerk, entered service at the Hall of Assembled Worthies, stole books from the hall to read, and for six years did not leave his door, until there was nothing he did not understand.

entries.zh: 及進士第，乃去隱中條山，與弟堦、域常易衣出。
entries.en: After passing the jinshi he withdrew to Mount Zhongtiao, often changing clothes with his younger brothers Jie and Yu when they went out.
entries.literal: After passing the jinshi he left and hid on Mount Zhongtiao, often changing clothes with his younger brothers Jie and Yu when going out.

entries.zh: 年長，不肯娶，謂弟曰：「吾與若孤煢相育，既娶則間外姓，雖共處而益疏，我不忍。」
entries.en: As he grew older he refused to marry and told his brothers: "You and I have raised one another in lonely orphanhood; once we marry, outsiders come between us; though we live together we grow apart—I cannot bear it."
entries.literal: When he grew older he would not marry, and told his brothers: "You and I have reared one another in orphan solitude; once we marry, outside surnames come between us; though we dwell together we grow more distant—I cannot bear it."

entries.zh: 弟義之，亦不娶，遂終身。
entries.en: His brothers agreed and likewise never married, remaining so all their lives.
entries.literal: His brothers agreed and likewise did not marry, and so remained unmarried all their lives.

entries.zh: 城謙恭簡素，遇人長幼如一。
entries.en: Cheng was modest, respectful, and plain; toward people old and young he was always the same.
entries.literal: Cheng was modest, respectful, and plain; toward people old and young he was the same.

entries.zh: 遠近慕其行，來學者跡接於道。
entries.en: Near and far admired his conduct, and learners' footprints lined the road unbroken.
entries.literal: Near and far admired his conduct, and those who came to study left footprints continuous along the road.

entries.zh: 閭里有爭訟，不詣官而詣城決之。
entries.en: When neighbors quarreled they did not go to the magistrate but came to Cheng for judgment.
entries.literal: When neighbors had disputes they did not go to officials but came to Cheng to decide them.

entries.zh: 有盜其樹者，城遇之，慮其恥，退自匿。
entries.en: When someone stole his trees, Cheng met him but, fearing to shame him, withdrew and hid.
entries.literal: When someone stole his trees, Cheng met him and, fearing his shame, withdrew and hid himself.

entries.zh: 嘗絕糧，遣奴求米，奴以米易酒，醉臥於路。
entries.en: Once he ran out of grain and sent a slave to fetch rice; the slave traded the rice for wine and lay drunk in the road.
entries.literal: Once he ran out of grain and sent a slave to fetch rice; the slave traded the rice for wine and lay drunk on the road.

entries.zh: 城怪其故，與弟迎之，奴未醒，乃負以歸。
entries.en: Cheng wondered at the delay and went with his brother to meet him; the slave had not yet awakened, so they carried him home on their backs.
entries.literal: Cheng wondered at the delay and went with his brother to meet him; the slave had not yet awakened, so they carried him home on their backs.

entries.zh: 及覺，痛咎謝，城曰：「寒而飲，何責焉？」
entries.en: When the slave awoke he reproached himself bitterly; Cheng said: "You drank because you were cold—what fault is that?"
entries.literal: When he awoke he reproached himself bitterly and apologized; Cheng said: "You drank because you were cold—what blame is there?"

entries.zh: 寡妹依城居，其子四十餘，癡不知人，城常負以出入。
entries.en: A widowed younger sister lived with Cheng; her son was past forty, feeble-minded and knowing no one, yet Cheng often carried him when he went out.
entries.literal: A widowed younger sister lived with Cheng; her son was more than forty, an idiot who knew no one, yet Cheng often carried him when going out.

entries.zh: 始，妹之夫客死遠方，城與弟行千里，負其柩歸葬。
entries.en: At first her husband had died far from home; Cheng and his brother traveled a thousand li and carried the coffin home for burial.
entries.literal: At first her husband had died as a guest far away; Cheng and his brother traveled a thousand li and carried the coffin home for burial.

entries.zh: 歲饑，屏跡不過鄰裏，屑榆為粥，講論不輟。
entries.en: In famine years he would not even cross to neighboring lanes, ground elm bark into porridge, and never ceased his lectures.
entries.literal: In years of famine he kept his traces from crossing even the neighboring lanes, ground elm bark into porridge, and never ceased his lectures.

entries.zh: 有奴都兒化其德，亦方介自約。
entries.en: A slave named Du'er was transformed by his virtue and likewise held himself to strict restraint.
entries.literal: A slave named Du'er was transformed by his virtue and likewise held himself to strict self-restraint.

entries.zh: 或哀其餒，與之食，不納。
entries.en: When some pitied his hunger and offered him food, he would not accept.
entries.literal: When some pitied his hunger and offered him food, he would not accept.

entries.zh: 後致糠核數杯，乃受。
entries.en: Later they brought a few cups of chaff and grain; only then did he accept.
entries.literal: Later they brought several cups of chaff and grain; only then did he accept.

entries.zh: 山東節度府聞城義者，發使遺五百縑，戒使者不令返。
entries.en: The eastern circuit headquarters heard of Cheng's righteousness and sent an envoy with five hundred bolts of silk, ordering him not to return.
entries.literal: The eastern circuit military headquarters heard of Cheng's righteousness and sent an envoy with five hundred bolts of silk, instructing the envoy not to return.

entries.zh: 城固辭，使者委而去，城置之未嘗發。
entries.en: Cheng firmly declined; the envoy left the silk and departed; Cheng set it aside and never opened it.
entries.literal: Cheng firmly declined; the envoy left it and departed; Cheng set it aside and never opened it.

entries.zh: 會里人鄭俶欲葬親，貸於人無得，城知其然，舉縑與之。
entries.en: When his neighbor Zheng Chu wished to bury his kin but could borrow from no one, Cheng, knowing this, gave him all the silk.
entries.literal: When a neighbor, Zheng Chu, wished to bury his kin but could borrow from no one, Cheng, knowing this, gave him all the silk.

entries.zh: 俶既葬，還曰：「蒙君子之施，願為奴以償德。」
entries.en: After the burial Chu returned and said: "I have received the gentleman's kindness and wish to become your slave to repay it."
entries.literal: After the burial Chu returned and said: "I received the gentleman's gift and wish to become your slave to repay this virtue."

entries.zh: 城曰：「吾子非也，能同我為學乎？」
entries.en: Cheng said: "You are not that sort of man—will you study together with me?"
entries.literal: Cheng said: "You are not that sort of man—can you study together with me?"

entries.zh: 俶泣謝，即教以書，俶不能業，城更徙遠阜，使顓其習。
entries.en: Chu wept and thanked him; Cheng taught him to write. When Chu could not master it, Cheng moved him to a remote hill and had him focus on his studies.
entries.literal: Chu wept and thanked him; Cheng thereupon taught him to write. Chu could not master it, so Cheng moved farther to a remote hill and had him focus on his studies.

entries.zh: 學如初，慚，縊而死。
entries.en: His progress was still as before; ashamed, he hanged himself.
entries.literal: His studies were as before; ashamed, he hanged himself and died.

entries.zh: 城驚且哭，厚自咎，為服緦麻瘞之。
entries.en: Cheng was startled and wept, blamed himself deeply, wore mourning hemp, and buried him.
entries.literal: Cheng was startled and wept, blamed himself deeply, wore the hemp of mourning, and buried him.

entries.zh: 朱全忠已篡，召為禮部尚書，不起。
entries.en: After Zhu Quanzhong had usurped power he summoned Tu as director of the Ministry of Rites, but Tu would not rise.
entries.literal: After Zhu Quanzhong had usurped power he summoned Tu as Director of the Ministry of Rites, but Tu would not rise.

entries.zh: 哀帝弒，圖聞，不食而卒，年七十二。
entries.en: When Emperor Ai was murdered, Tu heard of it, stopped eating, and died at seventy-two.
entries.literal: When Emperor Ai was murdered, Tu heard of it, stopped eating, and died at seventy-two.

entries.zh: 圖無子，以甥為嗣，嘗為御史所劾，昭宗不責也。
entries.en: Tu had no sons and made a nephew his heir; once he was impeached by a censor but Emperor Zhaozong did not punish him.
entries.literal: Tu had no sons and made a nephew his heir; once he was impeached by a censor but Emperor Zhaozong did not punish him.

entries.zh: 元德秀
entries.en: Yuan Dexiu
entries.literal: Yuan Dexiu

entries.zh: 初，穎達與顏師古、司馬才章、王恭、王琰受詔撰《五經》義訓凡百餘篇，號《義贊》，詔改為《正義》雲。
entries.en: Earlier, Yingda had joined Yan Shigu, Sima Caizhang, Wang Gong, and Wang Yan in compiling more than one hundred chapters of exegesis on the Five Classics under the title Yizan; an edict renamed the work Zhengyi.
entries.literal: At first Yingda together with Yan Shigu, Sima Caizhang, Wang Gong, and Wang Yan received orders to compile exegesis on the Five Classics totaling more than one hundred chapters, titled Yizan; an edict changed it to Zhengyi.

entries.zh: 雖包貫異家為詳博，然其中不能無謬冗，博士馬嘉運駁正其失，至相譏詆。
entries.en: Although the work embraced many schools and was exhaustive, it could not avoid error and redundancy; Erudite Ma Jiayun attacked its mistakes, and the two sides exchanged ridicule and slander.
entries.literal: Though it encompassed divergent schools and was detailed and broad, within it there could not but be errors and redundancy; Erudite Ma Jiayun refuted and corrected its faults, to the point of mutual ridicule and slander.

entries.zh: 有詔更令裁定，功未就。
entries.en: An edict ordered another round of revision, but the task was never finished.
entries.literal: An edict again ordered it to be examined and fixed; the work was not completed.

entries.zh: 永徽二年，詔中書門下與國子三館博士、弘文館學士考正之，於是尚書左僕射於誌寧、右僕射張行成、侍中高季輔就加增損，書始布下。
entries.en: In the second year of Yonghui, the Secretariat and Chancellery, together with erudites of the three academies and Hongwen academicians, reviewed the text. Left Vice Minister Yu Zhining, Right Vice Minister Zhang Xingcheng, and Attendant Gao Jifu then revised it further, and the book was finally issued.
entries.literal: In the second year of Yonghui, the Secretariat and Chancellery together with erudites of the three academies of the Directorate of Education and academicians of the Hongwen Hall examined and corrected it; thereupon Left Pushe Yu Zhining, Right Pushe Zhang Xingcheng, and Attendant Gao Jifu added and subtracted, and the book was finally promulgated.

entries.zh: 孫齊丘，歷監察御史、朔方節度使，終東都留守，謚曰貞獻。
entries.en: His grandson Qiqiu successively served as Censor, Military Commissioner of Shuofang, and ended as Guardian of the Eastern Capital, his posthumous title was Zhenxian.
entries.literal: His grandson Qiqiu successively served as Censor, Military Commissioner of Shuofang, and ended as Guardian of the Eastern Capital; his posthumous title was Zhenxian.

entries.zh: 子鎰，別有傳。
entries.en: His son Yi is treated in a separate biography.
entries.literal: His son Yi has a separate biography.

entries.zh: 儒學上
entries.en: Confucian Scholars, Part One
entries.literal: Confucian Scholars, Part One

entries.zh: 自輔國徙太上皇，天下疾之，帝在東宮積不平。
entries.en: From the time Fuguo moved the retired emperor, the realm hated him; the emperor, while still crown prince in the Eastern Palace, had long nursed resentment.
entries.literal: From the time Fuguo moved the Retired Emperor, the realm hated him; the Emperor, while still in the Eastern Palace, had long nursed resentment.

entries.zh: 既嗣位，不欲顯戮，遣俠者夜刺殺之，年五十九，抵其首混中，殊右臂，告泰陵。
entries.en: Once on the throne, unwilling to execute him openly, he sent bravos to stab him to death by night. Fuguo was fifty-nine. His head was placed in one vessel and his right arm severed and set apart; the deed was reported at Tailing.
entries.literal: Once he succeeded to the throne, unwilling to execute him openly, he sent bravos by night to stab and kill him; he was fifty-nine; his head was placed in a mixed vessel and his right arm severed separately, and this was reported at Tailing.

entries.zh: 然猶秘其事，刻木代首以葬，贈太傅，謚曰鬼。
entries.en: Yet the matter was kept secret; a wooden head was carved for burial; he was posthumously enfeoffed as Grand Tutor with the posthumous title Gui.
entries.literal: Yet the matter was still kept secret; a wooden head was carved to substitute in burial; he was posthumously enfeoffed as Grand Tutor with the posthumous title Gui.

entries.zh: 後梓州刺史杜濟以武人為牙門將，自言刺輔國者。
entries.en: Later Du Ji of Zizhou had a military gate commander who claimed to be Fuguo's assassin.
entries.literal: Later Du Ji, prefect of Zizhou, had a military man as gate commander who claimed of himself that he was the one who had stabbed Fuguo.

entries.zh: 王守澄者，史亡所來。
entries.en: Wang Shoucheng — the histories do not record his origins.
entries.literal: Wang Shoucheng: the histories do not record his origins.

entries.zh: 元和中監徐州軍，召還。
entries.en: In the Yuanhe era he supervised the Xuzhou army and was recalled to court.
entries.literal: In the Yuanhe era he supervised the Xuzhou army and was summoned back.

entries.zh: 方憲宗喜方士說，詔天下求其人，宰相皇甫镈、左金吾將軍李道古等白見楊仁晝、浮屠大通。
entries.en: Just then Xianzong delighted in alchemists' talk and ordered a search throughout the realm; Chief Minister Huangfu Bo, Left Golden Guard General Li Daogu, and others presented Yang Renzhou and the Buddhist Datong.
entries.literal: Just then Emperor Xianzong delighted in the talk of alchemists and ordered a search throughout the realm for such men; the chief minister Huangfu Bo, the Left Golden Guard General Li Daogu, and others presented Yang Renzhou and the Buddhist Datong.

entries.zh: 仁晝更姓名曰柳泌，大通自言壽百五十歲，有不死藥，並待詔翰林。
entries.en: Renzhou changed his name to Liu Bi; Datong claimed to be one hundred fifty years old and to possess an elixir of immortality; both awaited edicts at the Hanlin Academy.
entries.literal: Renzhou changed his name to Liu Bi; Datong claimed himself to be one hundred fifty years old and to possess an elixir of immortality; both awaited edicts at the Hanlin Academy.

entries.zh: 虢人田元佐言有秘方，能化瓦礫為黃金，詔除虢令，與董景珍、李元戢皆介泌、大通薦於天子，天子惑其說。
entries.en: Tian Yuanzuo of Guo claimed a secret formula to turn rubble into gold and was appointed magistrate of Guo; he, Dong Jingzhen, and Li Yuanji were all introduced to the emperor through Bi and Datong, and the emperor was taken in by their claims.
entries.literal: Tian Yuanzuo of Guo said he had a secret formula able to turn rubble into gold; an edict appointed him magistrate of Guo; he, Dong Jingzhen, and Li Yuanji were all introduced to the Son of Heaven through Bi and Datong, and the Son of Heaven was beguiled by their doctrines.

entries.zh: 泌以金石進帝餌之，躁甚，數暴怒，恚責左右，踵得罪，禁中累息，帝自是不豫。
entries.en: Bi fed the emperor mineral drugs; he grew restless, flew into repeated rages, and blamed those around him until one after another they were punished. The inner palace was filled with sighs, and from then on the emperor was unwell.
entries.literal: Bi presented the Emperor with mineral drugs as food; he grew very restless, often flew into rage, angrily blamed those around him, and one after another they were punished; the inner palace was filled with sighs, and from this the Emperor was unwell.

entries.zh: 十五年，罷元會，群臣危恐，會義成劉悟來朝，賜對麟德殿，悟出曰：「上體平矣。」
entries.en: In the fifteenth year the New Year's audience was canceled and the ministers were fearful. When Liu Wu of Yicheng came to court and was granted audience in Linde Hall, he said on leaving, "His Majesty's condition is stable."
entries.literal: In the fifteenth year the New Year's audience was canceled; the ministers were fearful; when Liu Wu of Yicheng came to court and was granted audience in Linde Hall, Wu on leaving said, "His Majesty's condition is stable."

entries.zh: 內外乃安。
entries.en: Court and capital were then reassured.
entries.literal: Inside and outside the court were then reassured.

entries.zh: 是夜，守澄與內常侍陳弘志弒帝於中和殿，緣所餌，以暴崩告天下，乃與梁守謙、韋元素等定冊立穆宗。
entries.en: That night Shoucheng and Inner Regular Attendant Chen Hongzhi assassinated the emperor in Zhonghe Hall; citing the drugs he had taken, they announced sudden death to the realm, then with Liang Shouqian, Wei Yuansu, and others fixed the succession and enthroned Muzong.
entries.literal: That night Shoucheng and the Inner Regular Attendant Chen Hongzhi assassinated the Emperor in Zhonghe Hall; citing the drugs he had taken, they announced to the realm that he had died suddenly, then with Liang Shouqian, Wei Yuansu, and others settled the succession and enthroned Muzong.

entries.zh: 俄知樞密事。
entries.en: Before long he took charge of privy affairs.
entries.literal: Before long he came to know affairs of the Privy Secretariat.

entries.zh: 李克用引軍去，帝還京師。
entries.en: Li Keyong withdrew his army, and the emperor returned to the capital.
entries.literal: Li Keyong withdrew his army; the emperor returned to the capital.

entries.zh: 胤、全忠議，盡誅第五可範等八百餘人於內侍省，哀號之聲聞於路，留單弱數十人，備宮中灑掃。
entries.en: Yin and Quanzhong agreed to execute more than eight hundred men, including Diwu Kefan, entirely within the Palace Domestic Service. Their cries of grief were heard in the streets. A few dozen feeble ones were left for palace sweeping and cleaning.
entries.literal: Yin and Quanzhong agreed to execute more than eight hundred men, including Diwu Kefan, entirely within the Palace Domestic Service. Their cries of grief were heard in the streets. A few dozen feeble ones were left for palace sweeping and cleaning.

entries.zh: 胤以鎮人性謹厚，即詔王镕擇五十人為敕使，內諸司宦官主領者皆罷。
entries.en: Yin held that men from the provinces were cautious and steady. An edict at once ordered Wang Rong to select fifty men as Imperial Dispatch Envoys, and all eunuch supervisors of the inner offices were dismissed.
entries.literal: Yin held that men from the provinces were cautious and steady. An edict at once ordered Wang Rong to select fifty men as Imperial Dispatch Envoys. All eunuch supervisors of the inner offices were dismissed.

entries.zh: 於是追諸道監軍，所在賜死，其財產籍入之。
entries.en: Thereupon envoys were sent to recall the Military Supervisors from each circuit. Wherever found, they were granted death, and their property was registered and confiscated.
entries.literal: Thereupon envoys were sent to recall the Military Supervisors from each circuit; wherever found, they were granted death. Their property was registered and confiscated.

entries.zh: 詔以中官脅遷狀及全忠迎乘輿本末告方鎮，罷監軍院，咸視國初故事，以三十人為員，衣黃衣，不得養子。
entries.en: An edict reported to the regional prefectures the circumstances of the eunuchs' coerced removal and the full account of Quanzhong's reception of the imperial carriage. The Supervisory Corps was abolished. All were to follow the founding precedents of the dynasty: a quota of thirty, wearing yellow robes, and forbidden to adopt sons.
entries.literal: An edict reported to the regional prefectures the circumstances of the eunuchs' coerced removal and the full account of Quanzhong's reception of the imperial carriage. The Supervisory Corps was abolished. All were to follow the founding precedents of the dynasty: thirty as the quota, wearing yellow robes, forbidden to adopt sons.

entries.zh: 內諸司皆歸省若寺，兩軍內外八鎮兵悉屬六軍。
entries.en: The inner offices all reverted to ministries or directorates. Troops of the Two Armies, inner and outer, and the Eight Garrisons all came under the Six Armies.
entries.literal: The inner offices all reverted to ministries or directorates. Troops of the Two Armies, inner and outer, and the Eight Garrisons all came under the Six Armies.

entries.zh: 全忠還汴州，帝以第五可範等無辜，頗悼之，為文以祭。
entries.en: Quanzhong returned to Bianzhou. The emperor, considering Diwu Kefan and the others innocent, mourned them deeply and composed a text to offer sacrifice.
entries.literal: Quanzhong returned to Bianzhou. The emperor, considering Diwu Kefan and the others innocent, mourned them deeply and composed a text to offer sacrifice.

entries.zh: 自是宣傳詔命，皆以宮人。
entries.en: From this time forward, proclamations and edicts were all conveyed by palace women.
entries.literal: From this time forward, proclamations and edicts were all conveyed by palace women.

entries.zh: ◎宦者下李輔國，本名靜忠，以閹奴為閑廄小兒。
entries.en: Eunuchs, Part 2 — Li Fuguo. Li Fuguo, born Jingzhong, entered service as a young groom in the imperial spare stables in the capacity of a castrated bondsman.
entries.literal: Eunuchs, Part 2 — Li Fuguo. Li Fuguo's original name was Jingzhong; as a castrated bondsman he served as a petty attendant in the spare stables.

entries.zh: 貌佇陋，略通書計。
entries.en: Homely and awkward in bearing, he knew a little of letters and accounts.
entries.literal: His appearance was clumsy and ugly; he had a slight knowledge of writing and reckoning.

entries.zh: 事高力士，年四十餘，使主廄中簿最。
entries.en: Under Gao Lishi's patronage, he was assigned at forty-odd to keep the stable ledgers.
entries.literal: He served Gao Lishi; when he was over forty, he was made to supervise the stable registers.

entries.zh: 王鉷為使，以典禾豆，能檢擿耗欺，馬以故肥，薦之皇太子，得侍東宮。
entries.en: Under Commissioner Wang Hong he oversaw grain and fodder, exposing shrinkage and fraud so diligently that the horses grew notably fat; recommended to the crown prince, he gained a post in the Eastern Palace.
entries.literal: When Wang Hong was commissioner, he put him in charge of grain and fodder; able to detect waste and fraud, the horses thereby grew fat; he was recommended to the Crown Prince and obtained service in the Eastern Palace.

entries.zh: 初，遣大將劉悟屯陽谷，當魏博軍，疑其逗留，悟懼不免，引兵反攻城。
entries.en: He had posted Liu Wu at Yanggu to block Weibo; fearing execution for delay, Wu turned his army against Yunzhou.
entries.literal: Earlier he had sent the great general Liu Wu to garrison Yanggu against the Weibo army; suspecting delay, Wu feared he would not escape punishment and led troops back to storm the city.

entries.zh: 師道晨起聞之，白其嫂裴曰：「悟兵反，將求為民，守墳墓。」
entries.en: Shidao learned of it at dawn and told his sister-in-law Lady Pei, "Wu has mutinied; he means to become a commoner and tend our graves."
entries.literal: Shidao rose early and heard of it; he told his sister-in-law Lady Pei: "Wu's troops have rebelled; he will seek to become a commoner and guard the graves."

entries.zh: 即與弘方匿混間，兵就禽之。
entries.en: He and Hongfang hid in a latrine and were captured on the spot.
entries.literal: He and Hongfang at once hid in a privy; the soldiers came and seized them.

entries.zh: 師道請見悟，不許，復請送京師，悟使謂曰：「司空今為囚，何面目見天子！」
entries.en: Shidao begged to see Wu and then to be sent to the capital; Wu's messenger replied, "You are a prisoner—what face have you to show the emperor?"
entries.literal: Shidao asked to see Wu but was not permitted; he again asked to be sent to the capital; Wu had someone tell him: "The Minister of Works is now a prisoner—what face has he to see the Son of Heaven!"

entries.zh: 猶俯仰祈哀，弘方曰：「不若速死！」
entries.en: He still groveled in pleas; Hongfang said, "Better die at once!"
entries.literal: He still bowed and pleaded; Hongfang said: "Better to die quickly!"

entries.zh: 乃並斬之，傳首京師。
entries.en: Both were beheaded and their heads sent to Chang'an.
entries.literal: They were then both beheaded, and their heads were sent to the capital.

entries.zh: 棄其屍，無敢收視者，有士英秀為殯城左。
entries.en: Their bodies lay unclaimed until the gentleman Yingxiu gave them burial outside the west gate.
entries.literal: Their corpses were abandoned; none dared to attend them; a refined gentleman, Yingxiu, buried them outside the left of the city.

entries.zh: 馬至，以士禮更葬。
entries.en: When Ma Zhi came, he reburied them with full ceremonial honors.
entries.literal: When Ma Zhi arrived, he reburied them with the rites due a gentleman.

entries.zh: 初，師古見劉悟，曰：「後必貴，然敗吾家者此人也。」
entries.en: Long before, Shigu had met Liu Wu and said, "He will rise high—but he will be the ruin of our house."
entries.literal: Earlier, when Shigu saw Liu Wu, he said: "Later he will surely rise high, yet the one who will ruin our house is this man."

entries.zh: 田弘正之度河也，禽其將夏侯澄等四十七人，有詔悉赦之，給繒絮，還隸魏博、義成軍，父母在欲還者優遣，賊皆感慰相告，由是悟得行其謀。
entries.en: When Tian Hongzheng crossed the river he captured forty-seven officers including Xiahou Cheng; the court pardoned them all, clothed them, and sent them back to Weibo and Yicheng—with generous leave for those whose parents wanted them home. The rebels were deeply moved, which is how Wu won them to his mutiny.
entries.literal: When Tian Hongzheng crossed the river, he captured their generals Xiahou Cheng and forty-seven others; an edict pardoned them all, gave silk and cotton, and returned them to Weibo and Yicheng armies; those whose parents wished them home were generously sent back; the rebels were all moved and comforted one another, and thus Wu was able to carry out his plot.

entries.zh: 師道首傳弘正營，召澄驗之，澄舐目中塵，號絕良久。
entries.en: Shidao's head reached Hongzheng's camp; Cheng was called to identify it, wiped the dust from his eyes, and keened until he collapsed.
entries.literal: Shidao's head was sent to Hongzheng's camp; Cheng was summoned to identify it; he licked the dust from his eyes and wailed until he nearly died.

entries.zh: 悟素與師道妻魏亂，妄言鄭公征之裔，不死，沒入掖廷，它宗屬悉遠徙。
entries.en: Wu had long feuded with Shidao's wife Lady Wei, who falsely claimed to be a survivor of the Zheng clan purged into the palace women's quarters; the rest of the Li kindred were exiled.
entries.literal: Wu had long been on bad terms with Shidao's wife Lady Wei; she falsely claimed descent from Duke Zheng's campaign lineage, that she had not died but been taken into the palace women, and all other clansmen were exiled far away.
